en: The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Naga King Sagara, Scroll One.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Yuezhi Kingdom during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Chapter One: On Practice (1). Chapter One: On Practice.
Thus have I heard:

At one time the Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus—eight thousand in number—and twelve thousand bodhisattvas. All were great sages who had gathered from the ten directions; they were fully endowed with all virtues and had attained the various dhāraṇīs.
There was nothing they did not master, and their eloquence was most authentic.
They resolve all doubts and enter great supernormal powers;

they analyze the meanings of wisdom and the various perfections (pāramitās) to ferry others to the other shore, fully manifesting the state of a bodhisattva; their minds are fixed in meditative absorption (samādhi), praised by all Buddhas;
they travel everywhere to distant lands, flying through the air with divine feet, subduing and transforming all demons.
Discerning all phenomena, they know them according to their fundamental truth and perceive the source of all sentient beings;
they accumulate the factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma) and remain unattached to the eight worldly dharmas; they adorn their body, speech, and mind with great compassion;
and donning the infinite armor of great diligence, they do not grow weary throughout incalculable kalpas.
Acting as a lion’s roar to convert and transform those of external paths, he seals them with the seal of non-retrogression;
he thoroughly understands the profound and essential Dharma-treasuries of all Buddhas—
namely, the Bodhisattvas Mountain Radiance, Wisdom Mountain, Great Illumination, and Universal Retention Mountain Firmness.
...Sāgaramati Bodhisattva, Śailavarman Bodhisattva, Śikhara Bodhisattva, Śailadhvaja Bodhisattva, Śailarāja Bodhisattva,
Śilāgharṣaṇarāja Bodhisattva, Garjitasvara Bodhisattva, Varṣarāja Bodhisattva, Ratnavarṣa Bodhisattva,
Ratnaketu Bodhisattva, Ratnaśiras Bodhisattva, Ratnagarbha Bodhisattva, and Ratna...
The Bodhisattva Vidyutprabha, the Bodhisattva Ratnaketu, the Bodhisattva Ratnaśikhin, the Bodhisattva Ratnamudrāhasta, the Bodhisattva Ratnavighuṣṭa,
the Bodhisattva Ratnavyūha, the Bodhisattva Ratnāmbu, the Bodhisattva Ratnaprabha, the Bodhisattva Ratnasaṃnāha,
the Bodhisattva Ratnadarśana, the Bodhisattva Ratnakāra, and the Bodhisattva Dharmavyūharati.
...the Bodhisattva Pure King, the Bodhisattva Adorned Crown-Mark, the Bodhisattva Gold Light Ornament,
the Bodhisattva Jewel Topknot, the Bodhisattva Celestial Crown, the Bodhisattva Thousand Lights, the Bodhisattva Original Peril,
the Bodhisattva Illuminating Darkness, the Bodhisattva Moon Eloquence, the Bodhisattva Resolving to Turn the Wheel of Dharma, and the Bodhisattva Pure Golden Light...
Śakra, the Bodhisattva Constantly Bestowing Fearlessness, and twelve thousand bodhisattvas whose virtues were all likewise.

Also present were the great beings of this Bhadrakalpa, including Maitreya and Mañjuśrī, along with sixty great sages; the sixteen noble beings such as Acintya and Vimukta; and Śakra, the Four Heavenly Kings, together with the devas of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

The Yama Heaven, Tuṣita Heaven, Nirmāṇarati Heaven, Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven; the Māra-suta Dharma-teachers; the Brahmā King, the Brahma-purohita King, the Śubha-kṛtsna King, the Bṛhatphala King; the Mahābrahmā Heaven, the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven, and the Vimalaprabha Heaven, up to the Eka-bhadra Heaven and the Kāmadhātu-vihārin Abhadra Śakra-devendra—each with sixty thousand retinues; the Parvata-vṛkṣa Deva-king with forty-two thousand; the Malla-deva-king, named Puṣpadhara, with thirty-two thousand, together with the Gandharva-devas;
and the Anala-dāha Dragon-king, together with seventy-two thousand dragons.

The Garuḍa Kings of the four quarters, along with all other great honored deities—gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, phoenix kings, mountain and tree spirit kings, sweet-voiced spirits, and so forth—each arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling accompanied by their retinues.
Having completed their prostrations, they stood to one side.
The bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās came forward, paid homage to the Buddha, and each sat down to one side.

At that time, the Buddha was surrounded by a retinue of several hundred thousand followers; seated upon a high, broad, and pure lion throne adorned by the various devas, he preached the Dharma universally for the fourfold assembly.
The Buddha was amidst the assembly like Mount Sumeru appearing upon the great ocean; his virtue surpassed all devas, and there was no one in the world to equal him.
His radiance was towering and majestic, illuminating everything without exception.
Through the majestic transformation of the Tathāgata, there appeared in the sky at that moment a precious canopy, adorned with various rare jewels and pendants, covering the four quarters.

Countless hundreds of thousands of hanging pearl necklaces—stainless gems of blue, yellow, red, and white, as well as "illuminating the void" pearls—emitted light from their beads; the colors were immeasurable and beyond calculation.
A rain of various fragrant flowers fell, reaching as high as the knees; from within the void, the sound of great thunder arose, and a rain of many famous incenses fell.
Thereupon, the worthy Mahāmaudgalyāyana, receiving the Buddha’s sacred intent, stepped forward and asked the Buddha:
"This present manifestation has never before been seen or heard of; what auspicious omen is this?"
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
“Now the Dragon King of the Sea wishes to come and see the Buddha; therefore, he has first manifested this auspicious omen.

Before the Buddha had finished speaking, the Dragon King, together with seventy-two billion court ladies and eight hundred and forty million followers, all carrying incense, flowers, banners, streamers, precious canopies, and hundreds of thousands of musical instruments, proceeded to the place where the Buddha was.

Having finished prostrating themselves before him, they circumambulated the Buddha seven times. Each took what they held and scattered it over the Buddha, making offerings with music. Together with the ladies of the inner palace and their retinue, they stood before the Buddha and praised him in verse:
“Out of compassionate giving, you take pity on the world; You manifest yourself as the Eye for the world.
Though born within the mundane world, You are unattached, like a lotus flower.”

Bestowing peace and security upon the world, illuminating the three times while dwelling in this life, you understand all phenomena like the light of the sun; I bow my head to the Supreme One in the World.
With the ten powers surpassing generosity and morality, you have disciplined yourself and brought your retinue to perfection.
He burns away the darkness of afflictions and guides the multitude like a well-trained horse.
Bestowing the seven great riches and extending kindness to all sentient beings, he is the parent of all;
I prostrate before this supreme field of merit.
The radiance from the mark between his brows shines like the sun or the brilliance of white snow;
though Brahmā and the gods stand above, none can see the crown of his head.
From the Buddha’s face issues forth a great light, and those who receive this light attain peace and security.
Universally illuminating hundreds of thousands of lands, reaching even to the Avīci Hell;
his gentle speech is boundless, resolving the knots of doubt for all beings;
his voice pervades the heavens and the world, pure and free from defilement.
Dispelling the darkness of lust, anger, and delusion, He illuminates with the light of wisdom;
Bestowing peace and causing joy, He manifests liberation for all.
Unimpeded in his mastery of the three times, Seeking a peer, none can equal him.
Knowing the conduct of the multitudes of beings, you understand where the good and evil lead;
observing the fundamental natures of men, you perceive them all at once.
Opening their minds to bring about liberation, I bow my head to the Supreme among the Wise.
Hundreds of billions of Māras came to the tree seeking an opportunity against the Buddha;
yet by the power of his supreme virtue, vows, and majestic spirit, he subdued their evil minds.
Without anger or weariness, he guided them through the power of his compassion.
Making offerings to the World-Honored One, who would dare to be indolent or arrogant?
Contemplating that all phenomena possess nothingness, they are like empty space,
like lightning, mist, and bubbles, like illusions and mirages.
Fundamentally empty, they bestow the marks of conditions; reckoning them, there is no self.
They illuminate and reveal the dharma of birth and death; therefore, there is none who does not make offerings.
Thus, throughout incalculable eons, they have diligently practiced for billions of nayutas.
I have made offerings to billions of trillions of Buddhas beyond measure;
having fulfilled the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditation,
and wisdom through my noble vows, I prostrate to the Great Sage Hero.
Thereupon, after the Dragon King Sāgara had praised the Buddha with these verses, he stepped forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I wish to ask a question; if you would deign to grant me leave, I shall venture to set it forth."
The Buddha said: “It is up to you to ask.
If there are any doubts, the Tathāgata shall fully resolve them for you!”
The Dragon King, having been granted permission, leaped for joy and asked:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva eliminating all evil destinies?
What is meant by a bodhisattva transcending all difficulties?"
What is meant by a bodhisattva being born in the heavens or among humans?
What is meant by a bodhisattva never being separated from the Buddhas?
What is meant by a bodhisattva encountering virtuous friends?
What is meant by a bodhisattva who is always in a state of peace and security?
What is meant by a bodhisattva who always harbors sincere faith?
What is meant by a bodhisattva who has much joy and protection?
What is meant by the bodhisattva’s causes and conditions for rescuing sentient beings?
What is meant by the bodhisattva’s increasing and benefiting wholesome dharmas?
What is meant by the bodhisattva’s delight in creating the roots of virtue?
What is meant by a bodhisattva constantly delighting in the meaning?
What is meant by a bodhisattva not being attached to the five aggregates?
What is meant by a bodhisattva always loving the Dharma?
What is meant by a bodhisattva delighting in the joy of the Dharma?
What is meant by a bodhisattva never being weary of what they hear?
What is meant by a bodhisattva requesting further instruction and contemplating its meaning?
What is meant by a bodhisattva being able to practice what they have heard?
What is meant by a bodhisattva possessing the virtues of renunciation?
What is meant by a bodhisattva dwelling in seclusion and conforming to the precepts?
What is meant by a bodhisattva casting off the heavy burden?
What is meant by a bodhisattva constantly dwelling beneath trees?
What is meant by a bodhisattva delighting in dwelling in seclusion?
What is meant by a bodhisattva dwelling in solitary seclusion?
What is meant by a bodhisattva being free from all flattery and deceit?
What is meant by a bodhisattva possessing the wisdom of renunciation?
What is meant by a bodhisattva entering the profound and essential Dharma?
What is meant by a bodhisattva contemplating phenomena as being like illusions?
What is meant by a bodhisattva not falling into the view of annihilation?
What is meant by a bodhisattva not falling into the view of eternalism?
What is meant by a bodhisattva transcending the law of causes and conditions?
What is meant by a bodhisattva being free from all false views?
What is meant by the bodhisattva’s self-delight in supernormal powers?
What is meant by the bodhisattva attaining the six supernormal powers?
What is meant by the bodhisattva attaining the supernormal power of wisdom?
What is called the bodhisattva’s supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows?
What is called the bodhisattva’s manifestation of unobstructed loving-kindness?
What is called the bodhisattva’s unimpeded vision?
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s thorough understanding of the mental activities of sentient beings?
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s practice of insatiability?
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s discernment of the words of instruction they receive?
What is meant by a bodhisattva subduing the māras and their adversaries?
What is meant by a bodhisattva being free from all fears?
What is meant by a bodhisattva guiding those who would regress?
What is meant by a bodhisattva attaining non-retrogression?
What is meant by a bodhisattva reaching the patience of non-arising?
What is meant by a bodhisattva transcending all purities?
"What is meant by the purity of all the bodhisattva’s practices?
What is meant by the World-Honored One bestowing the prediction of enlightenment? The Buddha said:
“Excellent, excellent, Sāgara Dragon King!
That you should inquire of the Tathāgata regarding such a meaning.”
"Listen attentively, listen attentively!
Reflect upon this well!
The Dragon King said:
"Indeed, World-Honored One!
We wish and desire to hear it.
The Buddha said:
“A bodhisattva abandons all evil destinies through four things. What are these four?

A bodhisattva harbors no harmful intent toward sentient beings; they constantly protect the ten virtues; they do not speak of others' shortcomings nor treat them with contempt; and they examine their own faults rather than proclaiming the impurities of others.”
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four matters by which one transcends all hardships. What are these four?

He constantly extols the Triple Gem—the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Noble Sangha; he does not disturb those who delight in the Dharma nor create doubt in others; and he fully guides and instructs those who are hesitant.
This is the fourth.
Furthermore, there are four things that lead to rebirth among gods and humans.
What are these four?

Not abandoning the mind of enlightenment; teaching others to likewise not violate the precepts; maintaining a pure heart and aspiration; and preaching the sutras for others while giving rise to great compassion.
These are the four matters.
Furthermore, there are eight matters by which one does not depart from the Buddhas.
What are these eight?

Constantly recollecting all Buddhas, making offerings to the Tathāgatas, praising the World-Honored One, fashioning images of the Buddha, exhorting and transforming sentient beings so that they may see the Tathāgata, hearing the name of the Buddha in whichever direction one faces, vowing to be born in that land with a mind free from cowardice, and always delighting in the subtle and wondrous right wisdom of the Buddha— these are the eight matters.
Furthermore, there are four matters by which one encounters virtuous friends.
What are these four?
To be without pride or flattery; to always show reverence; to speak with gentleness and compliance rather than arrogance; and to constantly accept verbal instruction.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are three matters that should always be kept in seclusion.
What are these three?
To be neither harsh nor rigid, yet not sycophantic; to eliminate all greed and envy, and to feel joy on behalf of others when they receive offerings—this is the third.
Furthermore, there are five matters in which one should always maintain profound faith.
What are the five? They are:

the power of understanding the joy of liberation, the power of accumulating merit, the power of entering into retribution and response, the power of following the mind of the Way, and the power of governing and guiding the Dharma;
these are the five.
Furthermore, there are two things that bring much joy and protection.
What are these two?
Not abandoning joy, and not dwelling in anger or resentment.
These are the two. Furthermore, there are twenty matters that serve as causes and conditions for protecting the assembly.
What are these twenty?

Constantly believing in the Buddha’s teachings, one does not cling to external conditions; one protects oneself in all that one does, while understanding that what others do is their own to receive. Thus, phenomena correspond with phenomena and phenomena reflect one another. Regarding the retribution of good and evil, there is no confusion or lack of order. The mind is free from conceptualization, devoid of self and person, entirely non-existent, and without coming or going; it has no destination, save for the retribution of causes and conditions arising from the security or peril of merit and demerit. One thus guards against all conditions. All Buddhas and World-Honored Ones have achieved the Way and its virtue through purity, eliminating all evil matters; for this reason, we cultivate the roots of goodness. This is the twentieth [point].
Furthermore, there are two things that increase and benefit wholesome dharmas.
What are these two?
Knowing the three grades [of practitioners] and practicing without negligence.
These are the two.
Furthermore, there are two other matters. What are these two?
To take delight in creating the roots of virtue while not desiring any recompense is the second.
Furthermore, there are five matters in which one always delights in the meaning.
What are the five? They are:
non-attachment to forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and consciousnesses;
these are the five.
Furthermore, there are five matters in which one always delights in the Dharma. What are these five?
Not craving form or sensation; being intent on attaining knowledge and wisdom; and protecting all beings.
These are the five.
Furthermore, there are six matters through which one constantly delights in the Dharma.
What are these six?
They delight in the five faculties, not in the five desires;
they always delight in Dharma assemblies, not in worldly talk;
they delight in expounding the sutras, not in food and clothing.
One should always delight in contemplating the Dharma and not delight in impurity;
delight in practicing the Dharma and not delight in mere words;
delight in the Buddha-Dharma and not delight in the teachings of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
These are the six.
Furthermore, there are eight matters for delighting in the joy of the Dharma.
What are the eight?
One delights in expounding the Buddha-way and does not delight in the lowly and base;
one delights in the perfection of deliverance and does not delight in the paths of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
one delights in praising the four debts of gratitude and does not delight in what is contrary to the Dharma.
They delight in great loving-kindness and compassion, not in worldly affairs;
they delight in expounding the Great Way, not in the cycle of beginning and end;
they delight in lecturing on the profound Dharma and the root of dependent origination, not in permanence, impermanence, self, person, or life-span.
Delighting in the true dharma of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; not delighting in frivolous play; being free from thoughts of negligence;
and delighting in adorning the Buddha-lands rather than delighting in contemplating cessation—these are the eight.
"Furthermore, there are five things for which one never tires of hearing.
What are these five?
To possess extensive learning and wisdom, and to be keenly perceptive and insightful—this is to never tire of hearing."
They listen universally without weariness, resolving all doubts and never tiring of hearing;
they never tire of hearing because through hearing they awaken to and comprehend worldly toil, resentment, and hatred;
they never tire of hearing because through hearing they sever desire and eliminate the defilements and attachments of all sentient beings.
Because one hears [the Dharma] that is courageous and decisive regarding all doubts, one never feels satiated; this is the fifth.
Furthermore, there are two matters by which one observes the meaning and seeks to hear [the Dharma] without weariness.
What are the two?
To give rise to the practice of the noble ones' right view, and to attain the essentials of unimpeded eloquence and dhāraṇī;
these are the two.
Furthermore, there are ten matters that one can hear and then practice accordingly. What are these ten?
To know contentment with what is beneficial and to dwell in seclusion;
Body, speech, and mind are tranquil; his movements and halts are composed and serene;
whatever he hears, he contemplates with purity;
he dwells alone with few concerns, taking no pleasure in the clamor of crowds.
Constantly practicing vigilance through the first and last watches of the night;
revering and honoring virtuous friends;
and maintaining a sense of shame and moral dread.
He constantly protects all beings with great compassion;
his meditative concentration is equal to that of the noble ones;
endowed with perfected virtue, he rescues and protects both the heavens and the world through his wisdom.
These are the ten.
Furthermore, there are five matters by which one is fully endowed with the virtues of renunciation.
What are these five?
Having accomplished what was to be done, they shall no longer forget or lose it;
they shall eliminate the fetters of dust and defilement;
and their minds shall relinquish all attachments.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, do not speak of others' shortcomings;
having attained liberation themselves, they see those who are bound and preach the Dharma of liberation for them;
these are the five.
Furthermore, there are five ways for those who have left the household life to accord with the precepts.

What are these five? To rescue and accord with the prohibitive Dharma by rescuing those who have violated the precepts; to accord with all that has been heard by rescuing those who have heard little; to accord with the concentrated mind by rescuing those whose minds are distracted; to accord with wisdom by rescuing those with evil understanding; and to accord with the knowledge of deliverance by establishing the multitude in peace and unconditioned liberation.
These are the five. Furthermore, there are five things to be abandoned.
What are the five?

To cast off the heavy burden and eliminate the five aggregates; to sever the fetters of affection and all habitual tendencies; to always abide in tranquil concentration and relinquish even quiescence; to enter the Way of Virtue and practice the Eightfold Path; and to enter the Noble Truths and establish all people in the Dharma of the True Truth—these are the five.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which one constantly dwells beneath trees.
What are these four?
Not begrudging one’s body or life; practicing all virtuous and wholesome dharmas; developing supernormal powers and wisdom; and performing tranquil deeds so that devas and humans rejoice.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four matters for delighting in dwelling in seclusion.
What are the four?
To dwell in seclusion while giving rise to great compassion is praised by all Buddhas;
to desire to save sentient beings without partiality or deviant conduct;
and when sitting to achieve Buddhahood, to be adorned with mastery and freedom, untainted by worldly toil.

To study the ultimate practices of other bodhisattvas, to accumulate the virtues of secluded dwelling, and to enter cities, districts, counties, towns, and villages to preach the Dharma for the multitude;
this is the fourth.

Furthermore, there are three matters for practicing *śamatha* (tranquil sitting), which are the most honored, unsurpassed, subtle, and wondrous merits, constituting the conduct of the noble ones (*ārya*).
What are these three?
Not practicing hatred or attachment, nor having any longing;
To be sovereign and free from desire, with a mind unbound by attachment;
to walk with freedom, maintaining equanimity toward all, and swiftly attaining concentration—
these are the three.
Furthermore, there are three things that free one from all flattery and deceit:
a mind that is upright and free from resentment; abiding in practice; and the severance of all fetters.
These are the three.
Furthermore, there are eight matters that fully embody the virtues of one who has left the household life.

What are these eight? They are: being noble and holy with contentment while dwelling in solitude; knowing the limits of moderation; attaining extensive learning; abandoning resentment through patience; not forsaking the mind set on enlightenment; practicing the four foundations of mindfulness; concentrating the mind with single-minded diligence in accordance with wisdom; and making practice the essential core of all that is undertaken.
These are the eight.
Furthermore, there are ten matters for entering the profound and essential Dharma.
What are these ten?

One sees that the body is naturally such and all phenomena are naturally such; the body enters into purity and all phenomena are pure. Having seen this, there is no "I" and all phenomena are without self. One observes for oneself that the body is empty and does not doubt that all phenomena are empty. One's own body has no sound and all phenomena are like echoes. One examines the body as silent and all phenomena as still. Regarding the "self," one scrutinizes the truths of all phenomena with precision. One’s aspiration is profound and subtle, seeing the depths of all phenomena. One's own body hears nothing and all phenomena are like the deaf. I have nothing received, seeing that among all phenomena there is nothing to be grasped. These are the ten.
Furthermore, there are ten matters:
all phenomena are like illusions, giving rise to the characteristics of deception and fraud;
all phenomena are like dreams, wherein what is seen has no reality.
All dharmas are like a mirage, for due to the arising of inverted perceptions, one sees what is not real;
all dharmas are like a shadow, for the causes and conditions that produce them cannot be taken as joy;
all dharmas are like the moon in water, for they cannot be grasped and their characteristics are detached from action.
All phenomena are like echoes, empty from beginning to end;
all phenomena are like flashes of lightning, appearing brilliantly only to vanish immediately;
all phenomena are like paintings, free from lust, anger, and delusion.
All phenomena are fundamentally pure and are not defiled by adventitious stains;
all phenomena are like space, arising and immediately ceasing without any fixed location—
this is the tenth.
Furthermore, there are two things that prevent one from falling into the view of annihilationism. What are these two? They are:
wisdom that accords with the times, which enters into both transgression and merit; and the clear discernment of the luminosity of the noble wisdom of all Buddhas.
These are the two. Furthermore, there are two things that prevent one from falling into the view of eternalism. What are these two?
To speak with the wisdom that all things are impermanent, such that as soon as they arise they perish and the mind does not remain forever—
this is the second. Furthermore, there are four matters that transcend the law of causes and conditions.

What are the four? The habituation to lack of wisdom leads to the habituation to birth and death; once lack of wisdom is extinguished, birth and death are eliminated. One does not fall into the view of annihilation, nor does one abide in the contemplation of permanence.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four matters by which one is free from all false views.
What are these four?

Understanding the wisdom of emptiness, one does not perceive self or other; comprehending signlessness, one does not perceive a life-span; realizing wishlessness, one does not perceive the three spheres; and discerning dependent origination, one is free from permanence and impermanence.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are six matters by which one enjoys oneself through the various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
What are the six?
By not looking upon sentient beings with malevolent eyes, one attains the purity of the divine eye;
by being able to endure harsh sounds when hearing them, one attains the purity of the divine ear;
and by having a mind that is undisturbed, one attains the purity of knowing the minds of others.
Planting the roots of all virtues, one then recognizes past events;
as the speech of the mouth is, so too are the actions of the body, thereby attaining the purity of the divine feet (*ṛddhipāda*);
practicing all forms of reverence and not deceiving the Dharma Master, one exhausts all outflows (*āsrava*) to attain purity.
These are the six. Furthermore, there are six matters by which one attains the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*). What are these six?
By lighting lamps, one attains the purity of the divine eye;
by offering music, one attains the purity of the divine ear;
by giving without expectation, one understands the minds of sentient beings.
Planting the roots of all virtues, he knows the events of the past;
casting off all hindrances and veils, he resolves all doubts and attains the purity of the divine feet;
through the gift of Dharma, he exhausts all outflows and attains purity.
These are the six.
Furthermore, there are six matters by which one attains supernormal wisdom.
What are these six?
Upon seeing the Tathāgata, one attains the purity of the divine eye;
upon attending the assembly where the Dharma is preached, one attains the purity of the divine ear;
by subduing the mind, one perceives the intentions of sentient beings.
By constantly practicing the six recollections, one attains the knowledge of past lives;
by abandoning all greed and turbidity, one achieves the supernormal powers of the divine feet, becoming light and able to fly;
and by following and cultivating all dharmas, one attains the exhaustion of all outflows.
"These are the six.
The Buddha further addressed the Dragon King:
"One may take delight in supernatural powers (ṛddhi):"

The Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, as well as non-Buddhists, seers, devas, nāgas, ghosts, spirits, asuras, the King of the Phoenixes, the King of Mountains, the Sweet and Gentle Spirit, humans, and non-humans—all those with the divine eye—when compared to the Bodhisattva’s eye, find it to be the most supreme, infinite, pure, and translucent. With the exception of the Tathāgata’s eye, there is nothing that the Bodhisattva’s eye does not see; regarding the light, color, and fundamental nature of all dharmas of devas and humans, it encounters no obstruction whatsoever.

Furthermore, compared to the ears of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, devas, nāgas, spirits, humans, and non-humans, the ear of a bodhisattva is supreme, infinite, pure, and translucent. With the exception of the Tathāgata’s ear, there is nothing the bodhisattva’s ear does not hear; regarding the sounds of devas and humans and the expositions of all dharmas, it encounters no obstruction whatsoever.

Hearing all sounds, he knows the matters of the three types of supernormal knowledge; he fully comprehends the minds of all sentient beings—the thoughts, intentions, causes, conditions, retributions, and cycles of coming and going; whether they are pure or impure, attached or unattached, and their various kinds of mental states:

whether the mind is contrary or compliant, bound or liberated, dependent or independent, deluded or concentrated, localized or non-localized, or whether it is subject to rise and fall. Having understood these clearly, he perceives the faculties of others and preaches the Dharma accordingly; through the knowledge of past lives, he knows the origins of self and others, reaching a complete understanding of everything that has arisen from beginning to end.
Sincerity that is not hollow, spiritual power that is independent, and the manifestation of all things—these are the five supernormal powers of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, the fulfillment of all that is enacted through mastery of the mind constitutes their enjoyment.
He manifests the body of a Buddha and enters parinirvāṇa, yet he does not undergo ultimate extinction.
What is called the bodhisattva’s supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows?

The bodhisattva transcends the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; his attained liberation relies upon the Buddha-wisdom. He clearly understands that all sentient beings are fundamentally pure from the beginning; thus, while he does not exhaust all outflows, he does not take realization as his own goal, but instead praises the exhaustion of all outflows for the sake of all people.
These are the six supernormal powers.
Furthermore, there are four matters by which one perceives unobstructed wisdom.
What are the four?
Cultivating the virtue of wisdom, they have attained these five supernormal powers;
practicing great kindness and great compassion, they understand the four modes of analytical knowledge;
honoring the wisdom of skillful means, they have reached the four kinds of unimpeded understanding.
"Concentrating the mind in meditative absorption on emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, one brings forth the dharmas of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment;
this is the fourth.
The Buddha again addressed the Dragon King:
"What is meant by 'the vision being free from hindrances'?
It means that all afflictions eliminate every stain;
and that whatever obstructions exist reveal the root of birth and death, thereby guiding one toward Nirvana."
Manifesting as those of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles, they transform beings until they reach the site of enlightenment;
following along with and exhorting them to practice worldly ways, they demonstrate to people how to act in tranquility.
This is called being "unobstructed."
Furthermore, there is the absence of hindrances (*āvaraṇa*):

manifesting all numerical categories up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), and manifesting the cessation of all numerical categories to reach non-attachment; although existing amidst the phenomena of conditioned activities (*saṃskāra*) that possess numerical categories, one encounters no obstruction regarding the dharma of non-numericality. Such a person, being free from the hindrances of the aggregates (*skandha-āvaraṇa*), attains the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and likewise encounters no obstruction regarding conditioned dharmas. This is called the Bodhisattva’s manifestation of unimpeded wisdom (*anāvaraṇa-prajñā*).
Furthermore, there are four matters by which one thoroughly understands the mental activities of sentient beings:
wisdom that accords with worldly conventions, clear comprehension of the objects of consciousness through meditative absorption, skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), and mastery over all phenomena;
these are the four.
Furthermore, there are five practices through which one never becomes weary or satisfied.

What are these five? Having attained great peace, one brings peace to all sentient beings; one's great compassion is firm and steadfast; one regards all people as one’s own marrow and bones; one manifests conduct in accordance with the conduct of others; and one establishes oneself in the most supreme and extraordinary virtues.
These are the five.
Furthermore, there are six matters for discerning the words of the teachings one has received.
What are the six?

Attaining dhāraṇī, the mind becomes established in stillness; entering into profound purity, the mind enters into all wisdoms; eloquence is unattached and uninterrupted, with the wisdom of skillful means leading to successive liberation—this is the sixth.
Furthermore, there are eight matters for subduing the enmity of Māra.
What are these eight?
To clearly understand that the five aggregates are like illusions; to be free from greedy views regarding sensory objects while practicing the work of emptiness.
Knowing that all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen, they guide beings according to their respective births;
they do not abandon the resolve for enlightenment, remaining firm and diligent;
they do not forsake the Buddha-way and have no fear of the triple world.
Detaching from all possessions, one contemplates persons and things;
seeking the wisdom of ultimate truth, one contemplates the mark of impermanence;
and one accumulates merit without weariness.
To gather wisdom and take no pleasure in the knowledge of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
this is the eighth.
Furthermore, there are ten matters for distancing oneself from all fears while performing the deeds of a bodhisattva.
What are the ten?
Practicing generosity with the thought of adornment;
establishing oneself in the precepts to sever all evil destinies;
They roam within patience, their faculties undisturbed;
they are firm and vigorous in diligence, never wearying in planting roots of goodness;
they practice meditative concentration, their minds remaining free from wildness.
They achieve wisdom and remain free from worldly defilements;
through skillful means, they clearly understand the vows of boundless noble knowledge and attain the discernment of phenomena;
they comprehend the meanings of the Dharma, and their eloquence flows in accordance with it.
Attaining dhāraṇī, resolving and eliminating all the doubts of sentient beings;
abiding in the abode of the Buddha, protecting all dharmas—
these are the ten.
Furthermore, there are eight matters that prevent one from regressing.
What are these eight? They are:
acting in accordance with one's words;
Reflect upon one's own faults and do not speak of the shortcomings of others;
rather than losing body or life, do not commit even the lightest or heaviest of transgressions;
do not rejoice in gain, nor be distressed by lack of gain.
With a mind free from malice, he guides all beings toward the intention of generating merit;
he impartially expounds the prohibitions and precepts, never abandoning the Teacher’s Dharma;
he brings peace and joy to the multitude, yet seeks no peace for himself.
To give away all that one loves without regret;
this is the eighth.
Furthermore, there are five things by which one attains non-retrogression from the unsurpassed, true, and perfect enlightenment.
What are the five? They are:
accomplishing the various perfections through skillful means without doubt;
entering the profound and subtle Dharma, and thoroughly discerning its definitive meaning.
With unimpeded supernormal powers, they discern the faculties of sentient beings and distinguish all forms of wisdom;
their conduct is free from attachment and inexhaustible;
they traverse dependent origination, yet do not exhaustively realize the cessation of all outflows.
These are the five.
Furthermore, there are three matters by which one attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*). What are the three?
To observe that persons are pure and devoid of self, that phenomena are pure and tranquil, and that wisdom is pure and unattached—
these are the three.
Furthermore, there are three matters that transcend all forms of purity:
The pure dharmas of the past are eternally exhausted; the pure dharmas of the future do not arise; the pure dharmas of the present have no abiding place—these are the three.
Furthermore, there are three matters:

the purity of physical conduct with flourishing merit; the purity of verbal expression with towering wisdom; and the purity of mental intention, remaining stable and unwavering in meditative concentration.
These are the three.
Furthermore, there are four matters by which one is seen by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and granted a prediction of enlightenment.
What are these four?
Having a disposition that is harmonious and compliant, and reverently following the Dharma;
Fully endowed with all practices, they contemplate pure conduct;
having attained the power of wisdom, they understand all minds;
they realize that the fundamental nature of all phenomena is primordially pure, neither arising nor ceasing, and thus remain undisturbed by whatever arises.
The Buddha told the Dragon King:
"These are the four dharmas practiced by Bodhisattvas, for which they are seen and granted the prediction of enlightenment by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.

Chapter Two: Differentiation (1). After the Buddha had spoken these words, twelve billion hundred thousand devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, humans, and non-humans all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
Seventy-two thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas;
one million four hundred thousand beings attained the purity of the Dharma-eye, becoming free from dust and defilement;
and eight thousand bhikṣus reached the exhaustion of outflows and the liberation of mind.
Five thousand devaputras became free from craving and desire.
The trichiliocosm shook in six ways, its great radiance illuminating the world everywhere, while celestial flowers rained down naturally from the sky.
The devas above played hundreds of thousands of musical instruments and together praised him in verse, saying:
"The Dharma taught by the Tathāgata now constitutes a second turning of the wheel of Dharma;
the wheel of Dharma that was turned at Vārāṇasī is now further increased and multiplied by this teaching of the sutra."
Why is this? Because for this sutra, it provides guidance and benefits for countless, incalculable beings.
If a person hears this and does not forget its root of virtue, how much more so for one who receives, upholds, and is able to practice it!
Having well obtained a human body, one joyfully beholds the Tathāgata and attentively hears this Dharma.
Having heard this Dharma, those who then resolve upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path close off the evil destinies and open the tracks for devas and humans.
"You should contemplate this comparison as being like the attainment of nirvana!
Thereupon, the World-Honored One praised the sons of the gods, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
Speak these words quickly!

Those who hear this Dharma of the sutra and rejoice with faith are established by the Buddha; they are those who have been transformed by the Mahāyāna. Such individuals shall attain the wisdom of the Tathāgata and be sealed with the seal of non-retrogression; they shall never again go to other realms, but will proceed directly toward the path of Buddhahood, transcending all suffering and hardship.
Thereupon, when the Dragon King heard this sutra being preached, he was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; a virtuous mind arose within him.
He possessed a maṇi jewel named "Pure Adornment of the Ocean-Establishing Universal Radiance," which was worth a trichiliocosm, and he offered it to the World-Honored One.

The light of that jewel eclipsed the brilliance of the sun and moon; the entire assembly, having attained what they had never experienced before, prostrated to the Buddha and stood there, praising him with one voice:
"A Buddha’s appearance is difficult to encounter, yet now that he has arisen in the world, he manifests such unprecedented dharmas as these!"
When the Dragon King Sāgara had thus offered the precious jewel, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By means of these roots of virtue, may I attain the unimpeded radiance of a Buddha’s body, and may that radiance universally illuminate all the Buddha-lands of the ten directions."
If people receive this light, their various afflictions will be eliminated.

Just as the light from between the Tathāgata’s eyebrows now causes me to thus dispel all darkness and attain equal enlightenment, so too shall those who have entered onto wrong paths be established upon the Right Path.
3. Chapter on the Six Perfections (1). Chapter Three: The Six Perfections. The Dragon King Sāgara addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva dispelling all darkness?"
The Buddha said to the Dragon King:
“The wisdom of a bodhisattva is extraordinary; they hold the lamp of wisdom in their hands, their wisdom is clear and distinct, and their wisdom is supreme.

They wield the sword of wisdom; whatever they undertake, they establish wisdom through wisdom, and they establish wisdom by means of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.”
Practicing precepts, patience, diligence, and single-minded concentration, universally contemplating all dharmas, establishing wisdom, and transforming sentient beings—
what is meant by a bodhisattva establishing wisdom while practicing giving?
It is equal to giving;
once giving is equalized, it is equalized with the self;
once the self is equalized, it is then equalized with others.
Having attained equality with all people, one attains equality with all dharmas;
having attained equality with all dharmas, one attains equality with all Buddhas.
Although there is giving, one does not abandon this equality.
Furthermore, just as that which is given does not follow after worldly defilements (*kleśa*), so too, at the time of giving, one abandons all defilements;
likewise, by abandoning all [attachment to] birth, one gives everything.
To be free from all views of abiding and to relinquish all that one possesses—this is for the Bodhisattva to establish wisdom and bestow it upon others.
What is meant by the Bodhisattva establishing wisdom and upholding the precepts?
To see that body and mind are tranquil is to guard the prohibitions and precepts.

Not relying on body, speech, or mind; not relying on this world or future worlds; being without internal or external; not relying on the aggregates (*skandha*), hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), or the sense bases (*āyatana*); not relying on the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), nor on *nirvāṇa*; and having no reliance whatsoever upon any phenomena—this is the guarding of the precepts.
Not playing with the precepts and remaining free from negligence—this is the bodhisattva’s establishment of the precept of wisdom.
In practicing patience, they do not apprehend a self, nor do they apprehend a person, nor do they apprehend both self and person;
they do not dwell in "I," nor do they dwell in "mine" or "my self"; they purify the person, purify the self, and purify the person and the self.
To see all phenomena as pure is the practice of patience (*kṣānti*).
Although one practices patience, there is no volitional activity regarding phenomena; one neither gives rise to nor extinguishes phenomena.
Although one practices patience, among all phenomena there is neither quiescence nor non-quiescence.
Although he practices patience, seeing that persons are empty and quiescent and devoid of a self, he is not terrified.
Although he practices patience, he does not apprehend body, speech, or mind.
Even if one's body were to be destroyed, its limbs and joints severed, yet one contemplates one's own body as being like grass, wood, walls, or fences, this constitutes patience.
Even if one hears evil words, abusive words, insolent words, unseizable words, or pure words, and understands that there is no locus for what is spoken, this constitutes patience.
Although his mind is distracted, his mind is free from fetters.
Since the fundamental non-existent mind is individually devoid of reality and perishes in an instant, to contemplate in this way constitutes patience.
This is the establishment of the bodhisattva’s patience of wisdom (*prajñā-kṣānti*).

He cultivates diligence to increase all wholesome dharmas, yet he contemplates the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) as neither increasing nor decreasing. He governs the dharma-realm with equanimity and examines all phenomena, yet he does not perceive any phenomena. For those who establish themselves in accomplishment and contemplate the world, [their views] arise from unreal inversions.

By means of the illumination of pure wisdom, he contemplates all phenomena without following them, without abandoning them, and without beholding their accumulation; he perceives neither coming nor going, for what could they come from, and where could they go?

Thoroughly understanding all phenomena and following the Dharma in this way, one discerns the matters of the truth of suffering and its inversions, preaching the Dharma for others and practicing with diligence.
Those sentient beings have no reality and no truth; if a person has nothing to attain, then all phenomena likewise cannot be attained.
Why is this? Because persons do not exist apart from dharmas, nor do dharmas exist apart from persons.
As the person is *svabhāva-less*, so too is the self (*ātman*) *svabhāva-less*.
The self is of the nature of spontaneity (*svabhāva*), and all phenomena are of the nature of spontaneity;
all phenomena being of the nature of spontaneity, the Buddha-dharma is of the nature of spontaneity.
One who seeks the Buddha-dharma in this manner, having understood spontaneity as spontaneous, shall attain the Buddha-dharma.

Whether there are those who seek, those who have already sought, or those who are about to seek, they seek this and have already sought it, yet find nothing to be obtained; this is the bodhisattva’s establishment of the practice of wisdom and diligence.
"In his meditative concentration, he enters into right attainment; he neither disrupts equanimity nor achieves it.
In his meditative concentration, through right attainment, all phenomena are without thought, without anything to be relinquished, and without any conjunction."

He practices unattached dhyāna regarding all objects of perception and establishes the various dharmas of dhyāna; he is likewise without confusion regarding the equality of all dharmas. He is neither body nor mind, contemplating the nature of meditative concentration; there is nothing to be practiced, yet he does not practice by means of dhyāna.
It is equal to original non-existence; through right reception (*samāpatti*), one attains equanimity regarding the originally pure dharmas. Being equal toward all people, one attains equanimity.
All dharmas are originally pure and equal, being without form; it is not by means of *samādhi* that one acts in accordance with what is appropriate.

The mind does not abide within, nor does it arise to wander without; consciousness has no place of dwelling, as it delivers all those who have fallen into inversion and transcends the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) of the five supernatural powers, the *śrāvakas*, and the *pratyekabuddhas*.
He surpasses wisdom through meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) to eliminate the vision of worldly afflictions;
he directs his vows toward the Path through meditative concentration to transform and enlighten sentient beings.
Thus, the Tathāgata remains constantly in a single state of meditative concentration until his final nirvāṇa; this is the bodhisattva’s establishment of wisdom-concentration (*prajñā-samādhi*).

"He contemplates all phenomena with the eye of wisdom, neither with the fleshly eye nor with the divine eye; having contemplated all phenomena, he sees that all phenomena are quiescent and observes that all phenomena are silent."
All phenomena are quiescent, without activity and without location;
all phenomena are serene, with nothing to be accomplished.
One universally contemplates that all phenomena are already thus.
To observe in this manner is what constitutes the contemplation of dharmas (*dharmānupaśyanā*).
When the contemplation of dharmas is thus practiced, one does not perceive any destination or point of convergence for all dharmas.
If there is one who perceives dharmas but does not contemplate them, they do not achieve contemplation through that perception of dharmas.
To have no seeking and no understanding, to neither know nor see—this is the seeing of the Dharma.
To be without self, without person, without life-span, and without vital principle—this is the seeing of the Dharma.

If a bodhisattva contemplates phenomena in this way, seeing that people are inverted yet still benefit sentient beings, they give rise to great compassion; such is the purity of dharmas, yet the multitude remains attached to them.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva gives rise to a vast and great resolve, desiring to deliver all sentient beings.
These sentient beings, however, are fundamentally without the category of "sentient being"; this is how the Bodhisattva establishes the Dharma of wisdom.
4. The Chapter on the Inexhaustible Store (1). The Inexhaustible Store, Chapter Four. The Buddha addressed the Dragon King:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva establishing wisdom and preaching the Dharma for others, yet not perceiving a person?"

A person has no self; there is no person apart from the body. A person is quiescent; a person possesses nothing. A person is fundamentally pure; a person is sound; a person is merely a name. A person is empty, signless, and wishless; a person is not something that can be numbered; a person is to be scrutinized with truth; a person is without birth; a person does not arise.

He preaches the Dharma for others, expounding on their purity; he harbors no sense of "self," nor does he conceive of a life-span or a soul. He does not destroy spontaneity, nor does he annihilate all that exists. He preaches the Dharma according to the fundamental conduct of each person.
How much more so for sentient beings, who are naturally pure, naturally selfless, and naturally formless—thus, persons are naturally so.
If persons are natural, then by this nature all dharmas are natural;
if all dharmas are natural, then all Buddha-dharmas are likewise natural.
This is called the fact that all dharmas are entirely the Buddha-dharma.
All dharmas are merely provisional names; they exist by virtue of being designated through conventional appellations. To speak of dharmas is, in fact, to discourse on what is not-dharma.
Why is this so? As it is with what is called "Dharma," so it is with what is not Dharma;
as one calls out the sound of Dharma, it is then not the sound of Dharma.
Why is this so? Because the dharmadhātu of all phenomena and their primordial purity are ineffable and cannot be apprehended.
The dharmadhātu is primordially pure and is devoid of anything to be maintained.
All phenomena within the entire dharma-realm are fundamentally pure; what could possibly be accomplished by destroying all phenomena?
This constitutes the Buddha-dharma and the teaching of the sutras.
For this reason, such quiescence exists, wherein there is no consciousness that perceives the transformative voice of the Buddha-dharma.
The Buddha-dharma has no teaching by which one may abide in either the conditioned or the unconditioned. Why is this?
Because liberation does not occur apart from the conditioned and the unconditioned.
"Could there be any other dharma that can be calculated or numbered? The Dragon King replied, "No."
“World-Honored One!
All dharmas are innumerable; the Tathāgata is innumerable.
The Buddha said:
"So it is, so it is! Just as you have said, all dharmas are innumerable and the Tathāgata is innumerable; thus, there is no duality between them.
What do you think, O Dragon King—is there any location for the term 'innumerable'?"
He replied, “No, World-Honored One.”
The Buddha said:
"For what reason?
You should know that one must cultivate this contemplation: the Buddha-dharma is without location and without words."
Just as the Buddha-dharma is without words and without location, so too are all dharmas without location and without words!
The Dragon King beheld the Tathāgata’s sublime and towering great compassion; such was his transformation of sentient beings, causing them to establish themselves in firmness.
Furthermore, all dharmas are without location and without teaching; yet the teaching of causes and conditions is proclaimed:

"These dharmas are with outflows (*sāsrava*), these dharmas are without outflows (*anāsrava*); these belong to the world, these transcend the world; there is attachment and non-attachment, the numbered and the unnumbered, the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); there are afflictions and resentment; there is the cultivation of this and the relinquishing of that; there are the dharmas of ordinary beings and the dharmas of the noble ones; the dharmas of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*); the dharmas of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and Buddhas."
The Buddha said, “Dragon King!
When the Tathāgata thus preaches the Dharma for the sake of people and explains its locus, he does not perceive any dharma, nor does he have any conceptualization of dharmas.”

Suppose there were a person who, in empty space—which is colorless and invisible—wished to paint various forms, such as celestial beings, human beings, elephants, horses, and foot-soldiers. Would it not be difficult for that person to paint these?
He replied: "It is most difficult, most difficult!
It is truly unprecedented."
"The God among Gods!
The Buddha said,
"O Dragon King!"

The Tathāgata performs what is exceedingly difficult: regarding those dharmas which are formless, ungraspable, invisible, devoid of syllables, and non-apprehensible, he nevertheless expounds verbal teachings for all beings and manifests written characters; to employ such skillful means is truly most difficult.
Those who have faith and enter into such a Dharma of this kind will accomplish much.
If there are those who receive this profound and subtle meaning, they shall not be given any opportunity by the various māras.
"Recall, O Dragon King, that in past ages I have again seen and served countless Buddhas, always leaving the household life to purely cultivate the Brahma-faring.

Those Tathāgatas never preached the profound and wondrous Dharma to me; rather, they taught according to the ailments [of beings]: the methods of giving, upholding the precepts, and training in the Path; the teachings on hearing, patience, benevolence, and harmony; and the merits of dwelling in seclusion, tranquility, and contentment."
Why is this? Because his practice and virtue were not yet perfected.

Once his practice and virtue were perfected, through a great and extraordinary radiance, the Tathāgata immediately heard this profound and wondrous Dharma, and at that moment attained the patient acceptance of accordance with the Dharma (*anulomikī kṣānti*).
For this reason, you should understand this meaning and contemplate it in this way: one who hears this profound Dharma becomes endowed with its merits.

Having received this profound sutra from the Buddhas of the past, they are free from the causes and conditions of conceptualization and names, as well as the defilements; they believe in, delight in, uphold, recite, and explain it to others as being without self, without person, without life-span, and without vital principle. The merit of such a person is exceedingly great.

If there were a bodhisattva who, out of compassion for all beings, desired to bring them peace and security, and caused every single sentient being throughout the trichiliocosm to attain such peace; and if all the devas and humans were to combine their merit and bestow it upon a single person—what do you think, O Dragon King, would that bodhisattva not indeed bestow infinite peace upon those beings?
He replied: "Very many, very many,
O God among Gods!"
The Buddha said:

"If there is a bodhisattva who bestows various forms of peace and security upon sentient beings, or if they explain to others even a single verse on the meanings of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self; or on emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness; or on the matters of no-self, no person, no life-span, no soul, and non-arising and non-origination—then the merit of bestowing such peace and blessing is difficult to measure."
Why is this? All sentient beings experience the peace of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), but they have never experienced the peace of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
He, by means of this profound and wondrous Dharma, expresses it through his voice, taking the peace of the unconditioned as his sustenance.
Therefore, a bodhisattva who wishes to establish their own doctrine and fulfill the aspirations of worldly beings should study the profound and wondrous Dharma.

If there is a bodhisattva present at an assembly who abandons the profound and wondrous Dharma to preach miscellaneous verses and embellishments, they are severing the transformative influence of the True Dharma.

Why is this? This profound and wondrous Dharma is spread throughout Jambudvīpa and shall not perish. Those among humans who hear and receive it, and those who delight in the Dharma, are not worth mentioning; non-humans are far more numerous.
If a Dharma master conceals the profound and wondrous Dharma, and those who read the miscellaneous verses do not delight in the deep Dharma, the devas will not be pleased, saying:
"This son of noble family!..."
He speaks of worldly matters according to what the world delights in. Alas, how tragic!
There is no one in this assembly who can preach the Dharma.
With a heart filled with resentment and grief, he withdrew and departed.
Then the Naga King Sāgara addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“Are the dharmas of giving, observing the precepts, and training in the Path mundane matters?”
"Is it not the teaching of the Buddha to leave home, go forth to study, and purely cultivate the holy life (brahmacarya)?
The World-Honored One replied:

"When the Buddhas appear in the world, they give rise to the dharma of non-arising. To act within the three realms for the sake of providing rescue and protection is entirely a worldly matter; it is not the word of the Buddha."

What, then, are these? The four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, the four formless attainments, the five supernormal powers, and the practice of the ten wholesome paths; generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, single-mindedness, and wisdom; writing, calculation, accounting, the study of scriptures and medicine, skill in pharmaceuticals and technical arts; the perception of the body, clothing, food, and wealth; and cherished meditative concentrations—all such activities within the three realms are merely mundane matters and are not the words of the Buddha.
The Buddha told the Dragon King: “When a Buddha appears in the world, there has never been heard before such suffering that is non-eternal, nor such quiescence that is non-self.

It is the meaning of abandoning suffering, severing the meaning of its origination, realizing the meaning of its cessation, and practicing the meaning of the path. It is entering the meaning of emptiness, crossing over into the signless, and being guided by the wishless. Regarding all conditioned phenomena, there is no arising and no production. This is the meaning of the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the faculties, the powers, the bases of supernormal power, the factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path. Seeking the true reality of fundamental purity—such as the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases which do not arise—is the meaning of emptiness and quiescence.”

Regarding all meanings derived from this, one does not destroy the various dharmas, nor does one destroy what is non-dharma. One understands that all dharmas are neither born nor grow, and that none of them arise.

One does not calculate whether things are permanent or impermanent; arising through causes and conditions, they attain the state of being unproduced. Returning to original purity, one leaves behind form and desire, manifesting countless dharmas as they enter the way of the Dharma. Abiding within the way of the Dharma, there is neither thought nor non-thought, neither correspondence nor non-correspondence. One relinquishes all notions, including the thoughts of purity and impurity. Without elevation or depression, the gateway to the profound darkness of the aggregates is naturally like space, and one attains impartial practice.

Regarding perception, conceptualization, and non-perception; regarding perception and the departure from perception—one regards them all as a single perception and departs from all perceptions. There is nothing to be observed, and all that is seen is stilled; all perversions are manifested as equal.
"It means that the attainment of the fruits and tracks is merely a matter of sound; therein is nothing attained, nor is there anything not attained, for there is neither acceptance nor rejection.
The Buddha said to the Dragon King:
"This which was previously described as the governance of all dharmas—the attainment thereof is beyond description!"
As for the śrāvakas, they attain the Śrāvaka Vehicle;
as for the pratyekabuddhas, they attain the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle.

The bodhisattvas attain the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), accomplish the unsurpassed, right, and true path of the Tathāgata, and become most perfectly enlightened ones.
This is what is called the Buddha’s word.
These words spoken are in accordance with conventional teachings; they are all the Buddha’s Dharma-teachings regarding ultimate truth.
The Way of the Buddha is without text; the Buddha’s words are without speech.
The Buddha’s teaching is traceless; the Buddha’s teaching is without conceptualization;
the Buddha’s teaching is without praise; the Buddha’s teaching is without transformation;

the Buddha’s teaching is without correctness; the Buddha’s teaching is without names; the Buddha’s teaching is without thought; the Buddha is without mind, intellect, or consciousness, nor does he have any recollection. This is called the Buddha’s teaching, yet it cannot be spoken, nor is there any verbal instruction, and it cannot be pointed out or manifested.
The Buddha said to the Dragon King:
"Teachings such as these are indeed the words of the Buddha.

The Tathāgata does not preach the Dharma by means of literal meaning; he preaches the Dharma without relying on written characters. Therefore, the absence of written characters constitutes the Buddha’s teaching."
The Dharma taught by the Buddha is not something that can be attained; it extinguishes all attainments. Therefore, there is no attainment in what the Buddha has spoken.
The sūtras taught by the Buddha have never contained verbal instruction; they are the cessation of verbal instruction. For this reason, it is said that the Buddha’s words are "instructionless."

The teaching of the Dharma is without grasping; it is a dharma without reliance, a dharma without negligence, a dharma without conceptualization, a dharma without arising, a dharma without destruction, a dharma without culmination, a dharma without attainment, a dharma without aspiration, a dharma without recollection, a dharma without activity, a dharma without discrimination, a dharma without existence, a dharma without destination, and a dharma without exclusion.
The Buddha said to the Dragon King:
"When the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma for the sake of beings, there has never been any practice performed nor anything realized!
All that I speak is fundamentally pure from the beginning; the Dharma has neither form nor color."
Therefore, O Dragon King!
That all phenomena are without form—this is called the Buddha’s word.
Furthermore, what is meant by the designation "the Buddha’s word"?
He understands all sounds and there is nothing he does not penetrate; therefore, it is called the Buddha’s word.
He examines the past, future, and present without any obstruction; therefore, it is called the Buddha’s word.
Because he has fully awakened to all speech, it is called the Buddha’s word.
Because he provides answers to all questions, it is called the Buddha’s word.
Because all that he speaks is based on causes and conditions, and his erudition encompasses everything from existence to non-existence, it is called the Buddha’s word.
One realizes that all that is spoken is like the sound of an echo; therefore, it is called the Buddha’s word.
It is without characters and without speech; therefore, it is called the Buddha’s word.
All characters and all speech are likewise the Buddha’s word.
Why is this so? These various syllables have been spoken by the Buddhas of the past, future, and present.

Because that which is spoken by the Buddha now, that which has already been spoken, and that which will be spoken hereafter—all these syllables and all the teachings expressed through them are called the words of the Buddha.

Entering into such categories and thoroughly understanding all wisdom is what is called the Bodhisattva’s discernment of the meaning of the Path; therefore, it is said that all written characters and spoken words are designated as the Buddha's word.

Not destroying the dharma-realm and resolving upon the wisdom of the single flavor—this is called the bodhisattva’s discernment of the sūtra-texts; therefore, it is said that all words and speech are designated as the Buddha’s word.

When one accords with and follows the wisdom of the Dharma, this is called the Bodhisattva’s discernment of accordant quiescence; therefore, it is said that all letters and verbal expressions are designated as the Buddha’s words.
When one speaks of wisdom that is non-localized and unattached, this is called the Bodhisattva’s discerning comprehension.
Therefore, O Dragon King!
There are no phenomena that do not return to these four principles.

When a bodhisattva understands these four principles, all words and expressions find their ultimate destination therein; wherever the body may be, there is nothing that does not lead one forward into entry into the Buddha’s teaching. For this reason, being unattached and fundamentally non-abiding, even if they were to speak for hundreds of thousands of kalpas, none could restrain them.
Why is this so? This is called the Dharani-door of the Inexhaustible Treasury!

“If a Bodhisattva attains this dharani, they shall speak inexhaustible phrases, skillfully conforming to the teachings; they shall cast off the defects of coming and going, responding appropriately without dependence; they shall adorn themselves with hundreds of thousands of true and wondrous phrases, enduring fundamental purity, protecting it from disorder, and understanding the equality of the meaning of high and low. They shall illuminate all afflictions and anger, enter into all practices while conforming to liberation, and according to the eighty-four thousand faculties, they shall skillfully expound the nature of things and preach the Dharma.”

If the sounds of the eight difficulties and all dharmas are inexhaustible, and even wisdom through analogy is inexhaustible throughout the three periods of time, could the fruits of retribution and the fulfillment of vows ever come to an end?
Can the sūtras be exhausted by following them?
Can that which the mind enters be exhausted?
Can the traces of ignorance regarding causes and conditions be exhausted?
Can that which accords with craving be exhausted?
Can that which arises from what is maintained be exhausted?
Can that which is spoken of as the station of the vehicle be exhausted?
Can the analytical discernment of the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) be exhausted?
Can profound and subtle diverse phrases be exhausted?
Can one reach the ultimate limit and exhaust them?
Can words that accord with or oppose [the truth] ever be exhausted?
Can the explanations of names and terms ever be exhausted?
Can the praises of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha ever be exhausted?
Can the True Realities be fully exhausted?
Can the categories of the Buddha’s Dharma be fully exhausted?
Can the karmic consequences of transgressions and blessings be fully exhausted?
"Can the discourse on the Infinite Deliverance (apramāṇa) ever be exhausted?
The Buddha said to the Dragon King:
"Because that which is spoken is called inexhaustible, it is termed the 'Gate of Total Retention' (dhāraṇī-mukha) for the Inexhaustible Dharma-Treasury."

Chapter Five: On Dharanis (2). Chapter Five on Dharanis.
The Buddha addressed the Dragon King:
"There are four dharmas that constitute the inexhaustible teaching and the inexhaustible treasury, serving as dharanis."
What are the four? They are:
the inexhaustibility of discernment, the inexhaustibility of wisdom, the inexhaustibility of clear intelligence, and the inexhaustibility of dhāraṇī and eloquence;
these are the four.
Furthermore, there are four things that are difficult to grasp, which constitute the inexhaustible treasury and serve as dhāraṇīs.
What are these four?
Their nature is difficult to grasp; the mind of the Way is difficult to grasp; entry into the Dharma is difficult to grasp; and entry into the conduct of sentient beings is difficult to grasp.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four firm and essential inexhaustible treasuries that constitute dhāraṇīs.
What are the four?
The firmness of one's vows, the firmness of one's practice, the firmness of establishing patience, and the firmness of transcending that which is conditioned by causes and conditions—
these are the four. Furthermore, there are four inexhaustible treasuries of teaching, which serve as dhāraṇīs.
What are the four? They are:

expounding upon all forms of ultimate sincerity; expounding upon dependent origination; expounding upon the conduct of sentient beings; and expounding upon the fact that the various vehicles are fundamentally devoid of inherent wisdom. These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four inexhaustible treasuries of light that serve as dhāraṇīs.
What are these four? They are:
illuminating the dharma-realm, illuminating wisdom, illuminating the clarity of insight, and illuminating the teachings spoken according to what is appropriate.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four further inexhaustible treasuries of the higher luminaries that serve as dhāraṇīs.
What are these four?
Exertion is supreme; diligent effort in the practice of the prohibitions and precepts is supreme; seeking to accumulate merit is supreme; and striving to gather wisdom is supreme—these are the four.
"Furthermore, there are four inexhaustible and endless treasuries that constitute dhāraṇīs.
What are the four?
Seeking the various pāramitās without end; not wearying of birth and death without end; transforming and delivering sentient beings without end; and seeking all-encompassing wisdom without end."
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four inexhaustible treasuries of insatiability that serve as dhāraṇīs.
What are the four?

To listen to the sutras before the Buddha without ever feeling weary or satisfied; to preach the sutras for others without ever feeling weary or satisfied; to seek the roots of all virtues without ever feeling weary or satisfied; and to make offerings to the Tathāgata without ever feeling weary or satisfied—these are the four.
Furthermore, there are four invincible and inexhaustible treasuries that constitute dhāraṇīs.
What are these four? They are:
being invincible even by all afflictions; being invincible even by all Māras; being invincible even by followers of external heterodox paths; and being invincible even by all enemies.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four treasuries that are without practice and inexhaustible, which serve as dhāraṇīs.
What are the four?

Not practicing the vehicles of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; not practicing the pursuit of all offerings and benefits; not practicing any forms of attachment or seeking; and not practicing any of the conduct of ordinary worldlings—these are the four.
Furthermore, there are four treasuries that are unattainable and inexhaustible, which constitute the *dhāraṇī*.
What are these four? They are:

not attaining what is produced; not attaining the conversion of those who hold evil precepts; not attaining the preaching of sutras as being superior within the conditioned Great Vehicle; and not attaining through begging.
These are the four. Furthermore, there are four powers that constitute an inexhaustible treasury, serving as dhāraṇīs.
What are these four?

The power of patience—enduring all that is done; the power of wisdom—eliminating the knots of doubt in all sentient beings; the power of supernormal knowledges—perceiving the thoughts in the minds of all sentient beings; and the power of skillful means—preaching the Dharma to all people according to their needs.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four great treasuries, inexhaustible treasuries, which serve as dhāraṇīs.
What are the four?
Not deceiving oneself and thereby ensuring the continuity of the Three Jewels—this is a great treasury.
To enter into immeasurable dharmas is the great treasury;
to attain all minds according to their respective aspirations is the great treasury;
for wisdom to be equal to space is the great treasury.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four further infinite and inexhaustible treasuries that constitute dhāraṇīs.
What are these four?
Boundless extensive learning, boundless wisdom, boundless fulfillment of aspirations, and boundless teaching of the Dharma in accordance with sentient beings—
these are the four. Furthermore, there are four matters by which a bodhisattva does not harm themselves and attains the inexhaustible treasury, which constitutes dhāraṇī.
What are the four?

Teaching the Dharma without self-injury; speaking with sincerity without self-injury; practicing in accordance with the Dharma without self-injury; and attaining the ultimate path without self-injury.
These are called the four.
Furthermore, there are four matters by which one attains the inexhaustible treasury of fearlessness, which serves as a dhāraṇī.
What are these four?
Not fearing the evil realms; not fearing assemblies; not fearing the resolution of doubts; and not fearing the loss of the Buddha-way.
"This is the treasury of the four inexhaustibles, which serves as a *dhāraṇī*. The Buddha told the Dragon King:

"This *dhāraṇī* of the inexhaustible treasury expounds immeasurable virtues, enters infinite wisdom, and gathers the practices of Bodhisattvas. Through the wisdom it provides, it brings radiant adornment to what Bodhisattvas seek; it is the Dharma-treasury into which the riches of Bodhisattvas enter. Entering the gate of *dhāraṇī*, one distinguishes verbal teachings, adorns body, speech, and mind, attains purity in all lands, and achieves sovereign assembly. One protects and contemplates the Right Path, enters among sentient beings to spread wisdom and guide them with the True Dharma, and through the power of diligence, fulfills the various *pāramitās*. One purifies the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and attains all Buddha-dharmas; this is called the *dhāraṇī* of the inexhaustible treasury."

Whatever numbers of names, titles, and designations there may be, as well as all numerical categories of dharmas, those who range within the True Dharma shall all come to take refuge in this inexhaustible treasury, which serves as a *dhāraṇī*.
When a bodhisattva enters this state, they make no distinctions among any syllables or characters.
All phenomena are pure and white, for their fundamental purity is indestructible.
They delight in all phenomena, for they do not violate the joy of the Dharma.
Because the ultimate nature of all phenomena is such that the phenomena toward which one aspires cannot be violated or deceived;
because all visual phenomena cannot violate the clarity of all phenomena;
and because the provisional designations of all phenomena cannot violate the realization of the Dharma.
Because they have attained all dharmas through unassailable diligent practice;
because all dharmas are harmonized and stabilized, remaining unassailed by the dharma of compliance;
