because when all dharmas are expounded, they remain unassailed by the radiance that incinerates all dharmas, for they are unassailed within the dharma of non-arising.
One has faith in all phenomena because there is no infringement upon the dharmas one holds dear.
One expounds all phenomena because there is no infringement upon any verbal teachings.
All phenomena are fundamentally non-existent because there is no infringement upon the dharma of non-destination.
All phenomena are profoundly true, for they do not infringe upon the equality of the dharmas of the three periods of time.
All phenomena are eternally abiding, for they do not infringe upon the immovable dharma.
All phenomena possess compassion, for they manifest as dharmas according to what beings originally delight in.
All dharmas are entirely equal, for they are taught without distinction.
One seeks the traces of all dharmas, for it is shown that all dharmas reach equality.
One reaches the destination of all dharmas, for it is shown that one enters the gateway of the profound path.
All dharmas possess supreme power, for they manifest all sublime dharmas.
All dharmas are characterized by ignorance and darkness, yet they manifest the clarity of wisdom.
All dharmas are gathered within, for they demonstrate that no dharma is ever lost.
They master all dharmas, manifesting them as inexhaustible;
all dharmas are quiescent, appearing as serene and tranquil;
all dharmas are empty, yet they manifest them as vast and universal teachings.
All phenomena are ignorance, because they manifest the root of delusion.
All phenomena abide, because they manifest the place where they are established. All phenomena enter into wisdom, because they manifest the state of being free from the dharmas of delusion.
Although all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature, they manifest for the sake of distinguishing all phenomena.
Although all phenomena are free from existence, they manifest for the sake of demonstrating the absence of any existing phenomenon.
All phenomena possess obstacles, yet they manifest the defilements of all phenomena.
All phenomena are constant mindfulness, yet they manifest the events of past lives.
All phenomena possess conditions, yet they manifest that all phenomena are subject to infringement.
All dharmas enter into the will, yet they manifest as the pacification of all disturbances.
All dharmas are most profound, yet they manifest as the dharma of being unmoving.
All dharmas abide in their places, yet they manifest as the locus of the manifold dharma-realms.
He is the guide of all dharmas, for he manifests the dharma of thorough discernment.
He is the realization of the fruit of all dharmas, for he manifests the resolve of non-conceptualization.
All phenomena are merely the aggregates (*skandha*); yet they are manifested in order to eliminate the suffering and afflictions of the phenomena of the five aggregates.
All phenomena are birth and death; yet they are manifested to show that all phenomena are free from defilement (*rajas*).
All phenomena are tranquil and empty, for they manifest that all phenomena have nothing upon which to rely.
All phenomena are as firm as adamant, for they manifest that all phenomena sever all attachments.
All phenomena are quiescent and extinguished, for they manifest that all phenomena sever causes and conditions.
The Buddha said to the Dragon King:
"This is called the *dhāraṇī* of the inexhaustible treasury of the convergence of letters.
When a bodhisattva attains this, they discern the arising of all written characters."
Just as written characters can never be exhausted, so too are the teachings on all phenomena inexhaustible!
Just as written characters do not emerge from the body nor from the mind, so it is with all phenomena: their location cannot be known; they do not abide in the body, nor do they abide in the mind.

For example, just as written characters have no basis upon which to rely, yet one seeks to explain and expound upon the matters of worldly afflictions (*kleśa*), and these [explanations] themselves possess no purity;

so too, when a Bodhisattva has attained the *dhāraṇī* of the inexhaustible treasury, although they speak of worldly afflictions, they do not cling to defilement, for they are ultimately pure from the very beginning.
For example, although written characters do not reside within the body, they are used to provide explanations for others;
so it is with all phenomena: though they are brought forth, the mind that teaches them remains pure.
Just as when written characters are spoken, they do not arrive anywhere, and when they are not spoken, they do not abide within;
so it is with all phenomena: even when they are spoken, they do not reach anywhere, and when they are not spoken, they do not accumulate within.
Just as letters have no form and are invisible yet exist externally, so too are all forms:
they are without form and invisible, yet they undergo transformation through the causal conditions of the mind.
Just as letters are empty, sovereign, and tranquil, such that they are all恍惚 (mysterious and indistinct) and without a creator;
so too are all dharmas: empty, still, and tranquil, with nothing that is created.
Just as letters do not themselves give rise to defilement, anger, or delusion, yet through letters there arise vocal teachings;
so it is with all phenomena: they do not themselves give rise to the delusions of defilement, greed, or folly, for it is from conceptualization that lust, anger, and delusion arise.
Just as one speaks of attaining the fruit and realization due to the conditions of various cravings based on words, yet words neither attain nor realize;

so it is with all dharmas: based on their conditions and oppositions, one speaks of the existence of fruits and realization, but in the fundamental dharma itself, there is neither fruit nor realization.
"Just as there are no phenomena that do not depend on letters, so it is with all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*); all phenomena arise from the Buddha-way.
Chapter Six: The Body of Dhāraṇī (2) The Buddha said to the Dragon King:
“The Bodhisattva already dwells in the inexhaustible treasury, yet seeks the Buddha-way through words and letters.
To master these words and letters is power;
to take refuge in these words and letters is the body.”
The image of cessation is the forehead;
entering the Dharma-gate is the crown of the head;
and contemplative observation is the brow.
The wisdom-eye is the eye;
the divine ear is the ear;
the speaking of names is the nose.
The brow-center where one restrains a distracted mind is the palace courtyard;
the gathering of all minds is the face;
and that which explains and instructs the minds of all sentient beings is the faculty of the tongue.
Stabilizing the mind is the teeth;
the vigorous lion’s gaze is the beard;
concealing empty words is the lips.
Contemplating all phenomena is the throat;
exerting oneself to deliver sentient beings and cause them joy is the shoulders;
being upright in what one says is the spleen.
Examining the equality of all phenomena is the abdomen;
entering the profound gate is the navel;
entering the left and right paths is the palms.
The integration of all dharmas is the arm;
the phrases of the ten wholesome actions that provide excellent protection are the fingers;
and the copper of the pure dharma is the nails.
Bringing forth thoughts of emptiness and non-being is the ribs;
preaching the Dharma in successive order is the spine;
and speaking without violating the proper time and without any ulterior motive for measurement is the buttocks.
Being fully endowed with tranquil contemplation is the kneecap;
tending toward the dharma of profound scrutiny is the knee;
and understanding all things is the calf.
The mind being tranquil is the instep;
traveling to the ten directions is the sole of the foot;
teaching the Truths in succession is the stride.
Knowing shame, modesty, and disgrace is one's clothing;
adornment with the garland of the Dharma is one's cosmetic decoration;
and the various flowers of the Dharma are one's bedding.
Teaching various dharmas is the pillow;
being without anger or contention is the scented ointment;
acting in accordance with what is appropriate and having nothing that is not understood is the blended incense.
Entering into profound precepts is its fragrance;
mastery over all dharmas is its retinue;
and extolling the tracks of Brahma is its kinsmen and friends.
Attaining a community of peace and security is one's circle of acquaintances;
severing all fetters and transforming the multitude is one's close kin;
and thoroughly understanding all matters is one's household.
A mind that is pure is the mother;
all skillful means that are without reliance or belief are the father, wisdom;
and the mind of various supernormal powers and insights arises from equanimity.
The perfection of giving is food and drink;
the perfection of ethical discipline is peace and security;
the perfection of patience is adornment.
The Perfection of Vigor is the diligent accomplishment of wholesome deeds;
the Perfection of Mindfulness is the state of full satisfaction;
the Perfection of Wisdom is conformity with the times.
The "Infinite Skillful Means" (*upāyakauśalya-pāramitā*) refers to the convergence of the meanings of these two phrases;
the "Factors of the Path" (*mārgāṅga*) and "Limb of the Body" (*kāyāṅga*) refer to their respective categories.
He expounds with utmost sincerity, never encroaching upon or deceiving others; though he is honored and free among all the world’s nobles and elites, he remains self-restrained regarding the Dharma.
The Buddha said to the Dragon King:
"This is the dhāraṇī of the inexhaustible treasury, which has no form or physical body!
There are bodhisattvas who, through this dhāraṇī, delight in the joy of the Dharma."
It is like a king dwelling within his inner palace;
like Śakra, Lord of the Devas, atop Mount Sumeru, majestic and awe-inspiring in his divine power;
or like Brahmā, honored, noble, and sovereign.
Like the Kāla-āsura dwelling in seclusion, he is difficult to restrain;
like the boundless ocean, his merit is transcendent and extraordinary;
like a great mountain of jewels, he is the delight of the devas.
It is like parents who have an only son, loving and cherishing him beyond measure;
it is like the full moon, shining alone among the stars so that all bow their heads in reverence;
it is like the World-Honored One emitting a great radiance for the sake of devas and humans.
Like the sun first rising, its radiance is gentle and soft;
like a peacock amidst the forest trees emitting its wondrous song;
like a lion in a rocky cave partaking of choice food and drink.
Like a dragon whose mind is harmonized, raining down at the proper time;
like a Wheel-Turning King who transforms the nation through the Great Dharma;
like the dance of many dragons, stirring forth thunder and lightning.
Like a dragon king who has attained mastery and brings down the great rain of Dharma;
like Śakra, Lord of Devas, who pacifies and transforms all those of external and heterodox paths;
like a valiant general who crushes and subdues formidable enemies, removes all weariness and defilement, and brings all Māras under submission.
Like water extinguishing fire;
like wind bending the grass; with the mind as the earth, he transforms and enlightens the wise and guides sentient beings in accordance with their nature;
like fire consuming grass, he endures all suffering and joy.
Like a wet nurse who nurtures the son of a great elder, healing all manner of ailments with a steadfast mind that fulfills the aspirations of all;
like the king of wish-fulfilling jewels, which encompasses all treasures.
The Buddha said to the Dragon King:
"Any bodhisattva who dwells in the dhāraṇī gate of the inexhaustible treasury may be said to have entered the bodhimanda of the Buddha."

Just as the great ocean contains all manner of jewels and precious treasures within its vast repositories, so too is this *dhāraṇī* an inexhaustible treasury that encompasses the expansive Dharma as a casket of the jewels of the Path; it is like countless caskets of incense that allow immeasurable people to have their every desire fulfilled at will.

When a bodhisattva has already dwelled in the dharani-door of the inexhaustible treasury, they transform and edify all beings through true and wondrous speech, causing each to attain their proper place.
This dharani enters into all sounds.
Those here who are named "Path-Mind" are called "Present Before One's Eyes" in the land of the Tathāgata Ekaratnacchatra in the world Ananta;
those here who are named "All-Pervasive Wisdom" are called "Universal Attainment" in the land of the Tathāgata Nāganāyaka in the world Atikrāntavimokṣa;
those here who are named "Perfection of Giving" are called "Essential Vitality" in the land of the Tathāgata Śrī in the world Praśānta.
This which is called the Perfection of Precepts (Śīlapāramitā) is known as Abundant Peace in the Buddha-land of the Tathāgata Free from Sorrow in the world Without Sorrow;
this which is called the Perfection of Patience (Kṣāntipāramitā) is known as the Inexhaustible Word in the Buddha-land of the Tathāgata Free from Defilement in the world Without Stain;
this which is called the Perfection of Vigor (Vīryapāramitā) is known as Supreme Crossing in the Buddha-land of the Tathāgata Stainless Light in the world Universal Radiance.
He who is named Dhyānapāramitā (Perfection of Meditation) has the Buddha-land called Śāntacaryā (Tranquil Conduct) in the world called Lokanāyaka-dṛḍha (Firm Leader of the World).
He who is named Prajñāpāramitā (Perfection of Wisdom) has the Buddha-land called Viśuddha (Pure) in the world called Varṣa-rāja (King of Rain).
He who is named Upāyakauśalya (Skillful Means) has the Buddha-land called Anuvartana-samaya (Conforming to Custom) in the world called Vimala-vinaya (Stainless Discipline).

What is here called "loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity" is, in the Buddha-land of the Tathāgata Śrī-artha of that world Abhyudgata, called "the mutual pacification of self and other through compassionate care.

What is here called "the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path" is, in the Buddha-land of the Tathāgata Mūlapratiśaraṇa of that world Anabhirati, called "the primordial source wherein all roots and origins are exhausted and return to the root.
What is here called "the four foundations of mindfulness" is, in another world, called "the non-abiding."
What is here called the four right efforts (*catvāri samyakprahāṇāni*) is there called the supreme excellence;
what is here called the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipādāḥ*) is there called the transcendent stride;
what is here called the five faculties (*pañcendriyāṇi*) is there called the source of joy.
What is here called the five powers is there called firm strength;
what is here called the factors of enlightenment is there called freedom from darkness;
what is here called the eightfold path is there called that which leads to deliverance.
This is called discernment, while that is called direct vision;
this is called protection and reliance, while that is called conformity;
this is called the gift of Dharma, while that is called skillful gathering.
This is called "tranquil contemplation," while that is called "concentrated observation";
this is called "gate of liberation," while that is called "freedom from delusion";
this is called "merit," while that is called "adornment."
This is called wisdom; that is called thorough understanding.
This is called renouncing the household life; that is called practicing cultivation.
This is called possessing the precepts; that is called being free from transgressions.
This is called "Peaceful Unconditioned," while that is called "Nirvana";
this is called "Praising the Buddha's Immeasurability," while that is called "The Buddha’s Eye Emitting Light."
The Buddha said to the Dragon King:

“Consider the various kinds of sounds, speech, and teachings used in all the Buddha-fields; if a bodhisattva attains the inexhaustible treasury, they will know all the sounds and written characters spoken and taught in every Buddha-field.”

If a Buddha were to spend an eon, or even more than an eon, praising the teachings of words, phrases, and chapters produced throughout the ten directions that pertain to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), they could not exhaustively convey the meaning of the sounds of all the Buddha-lands.

When the Buddha spoke this Dharani-door of the Inexhaustible Treasury, sixty thousand bodhisattvas all attained dharanis; eight thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti); and thirty-two thousand people all resolved their minds upon supreme, perfect, and true enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).
Chapter Seven: The Gate of Dharanis (2). Chapter Seven: The Gate of Dharanis. At that time, the Buddha addressed the Dragon King:
“By means of this, the Bodhisattva leaves behind all paths of darkness and proceeds toward all forms of penetrating wisdom.”
In the distant past, incalculable, immeasurable, and inconceivable kalpas ago, there was a Buddha.

He was named Brahmottaradevarāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, called Buddha, World-Honored One. His world was named Saṃcitaguṇa, and the kalpa was named Viśuddha.
At that time, the world of Saṃbhāradhara was prosperous, peaceful, and secure; the five grains grew spontaneously.
Its bliss was boundless, and gods and humans flourished in great numbers.

If the ten billion four-continent worlds of this land of mine were combined into a single buddha-field, it would constitute but one set of four continents in that land. Likewise, the hundred billion Mount Sumerus [of our world] are like this: the vastness and boundlessness of the world of Saṃbhāradhara, where the Tathāgata Brahmottara resides, is indeed such as this!

That world is like a vajra-luminous maṇi-jewel, naturally and eternally pervaded by great radiance; it is covered all around with interlaced jewels, draped with hanging silks, banners, and streamers, while hundreds of thousands of musical instruments resound spontaneously in the sky without being struck, their music heard throughout the entire buddha-field.
The sounds of those musical instruments do not produce voices of lust, anger, or delusion; they only manifest the sounds of the joy and delight of the Dharma, which is tranquil and serene.

When the devas and human beings hear the sound of this music, they attain single-minded tranquility and stability; they become peaceful and serene, no longer harmed by the afflictions of worldly toil.
That land is level and even, like soft cloth; there is no sound of the miserable realms, nor any instruction therein.
The devas and humans are pure and all understand the subtle and wondrous; they are intent upon the Mahāyāna, with few seeking the vehicles of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.

Whatever they think of in their minds—whether clothing, food, drink, or dwellings—all that they desire arrives spontaneously according to their will. Gods and humans are equal, with none suffering from exhaustion, distress, or lack. Their garments, food, and drink are like those in the Tuṣita Heaven; everything possessed in that land is uniform and without distinction.

The lifespan of that Tathāgata will be a full six million seven hundred and twenty thousand years, and the lifespan of the people in that land will likewise be so; there shall be none who die prematurely.
There will be seventy-two nayutas of bodhisattvas in that buddha-field, while śrāvakas will be very few.
"At that time, there was a Wheel-Turning Sage King named Anantapuṇya, who ruled over sixteen sets of four continents.
This King Anantapuṇya had eighty-four nayutas of consorts, who were like celestial jade maidens."
There were four chief queens:
the first was named Vimalā, the second Vimalaprabhā, the third Viśuddhā, and the fourth Viśuddhapada.
He had eighty-four thousand sons, all of whom possessed the physical marks of great heroism.
There were eight who were upright and handsome, all of whom were resolved upon the Mahāyāna.
At that time, King Akṣayapuṇya resided in a great city named Sukhāvatī.
That city was two thousand four hundred and forty *li* long from east to west, and its breadth from south to north was likewise the same.

The Tathāgata Brahmottara appeared in that land; King Anantapuṇya established a vihāra, planting a great forest of trees named Uparigandhaprabha, which served as the place where the Buddha dwelt and traveled.
In the center of the city, a royal palace was constructed, composed of the seven precious jewels.
Within the city, there were eighty-four thousand streets and alleys, and eighty-four thousand railings.
In each street and lane there were eighty-four thousand households.
The great city walls were sevenfold, with seven tiers of railings, seven rows of trees, and seven layers of intersecting paths; surrounding the city were ten thousand pleasure gardens for recreation.

Its moats were sevenfold in number, filled with water of eight virtues, where blue, red, yellow, and white lotuses grew, all possessing exquisite fragrances; ruddy sheldrakes, ducks, and wild geese followed one another as they called out.
Such was that city, with names such as these, immeasurable and inconceivable.
The King made offerings to the Buddha, providing for his comfort with all necessities fully supplied and nothing lacking, for hundreds of thousands of years beyond measure.

Leading his inner court, children, grandchildren, kinsmen, friends, associates, retinue, and the people of the kingdom, he went to the Forest of Supreme Fragrant Light to see the Tathāgata Brahmaśikhara; he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to stand to one side.
The Buddha told the king:
"There are four matters by which a great king, a gentleman, and a sagely sovereign may attain mastery, being unlike the common multitude, and thereby increase wholesome dharmas."
What are these four? They are:
establishing oneself in firm faith; frequently visiting the worthy and the noble; delighting in requesting instruction and seeking benefit; and seeking virtue while admiring righteousness;

finding joy in the Dharma by constantly contemplating the dharmas of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self, and observing that all conditioned defilements in the world ultimately lead to separation and parting.
One should restrain one's own mind, enter into non-negligence, discern the pleasures of desire, and harbor no covetous envy;
one should not destroy or sever the merits of past lives, nor abandon the aspiration for the Way, but instead devote oneself to sublime wisdom.
"These are the four matters by which a great sovereign of a nation may still attain mastery, being unlike the common masses.
King Akṣayamati addressed the World-Honored One, saying,
"By how many dharmas does a bodhisattva attain mastery?"
The Buddha told the king:
"A bodhisattva possesses eight qualities through which they attain mastery.
What are these eight?"
Having attained the five supernormal powers, they enjoy them for themselves, never regressing and remaining free from all obstructions;
they eliminate anger and resentment, harboring no intent to harm; they fully manifest noble wisdom and are gathered within the light of the Path;
having accomplished what was to be done, they presently attain sagely penetration, possessing sincere faith and divine feet, and have uprooted all that exists.
Through the noble relinquishment of wisdom, they abandon all the dust and defilements of false views and attain the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) established by the Buddha—
unattached and non-abiding; they are fully endowed with the bases of power (*balasthāna*), reach the inexhaustible ocean-seal samādhi (*akṣaya-puṇya-samudra-mudrā-samādhi*),
can delight sentient beings, and master all the teachings of the Buddhas to achieve dhāraṇī.
With a pure mind, they do not forget what they have heard; they preach the Dharma according to the needs of others;
they enter into the single flavor of meaning and abide at the ultimate limit (bhūtakoṭi); they do not conceive of a self, yet they do not give rise to the patience regarding dharmas (dharmakṣānti).
"These are the eight matters by which a bodhisattva attains mastery.
The Buddha told the king:
"Furthermore, there is a dhāraṇī named 'Precious Matters' (Ratnavastu); a bodhisattva who attains this dhāraṇī gains mastery over all dharmas."
At that time, the Buddha expounded for the king the wisdom of the *Ratnavastu-dhāraṇī*, fully analyzing its meaning for a full hundred thousand years.

The king abandoned all state affairs and every worldly concern, and with single-minded devotion, he and his retinue listened to and received the transformative teachings of the Way. For those hundred thousand years, he never conceived thoughts of desire, harbored no resentment, nor held any intent to harm. He disregarded his wife, children, kingdom, and kin; regarding all possessions, he never again entertained calculations of ownership. Wishing only for the joy of the Dharma, he resolved his will upon the Buddha-way, practiced great compassion (*mahāmaitrī*) with pure clarity, and extended universal equanimity (*samacitta*) and great pity (*mahākaruṇā*) toward all beings. Donning the armor of great virtue, he listened to and received the Dharma.
For a full hundred thousand years, such as these, he received the Buddha’s instructions; by means of this essential *dhāraṇī* concerning the jewel, his task was accomplished.

He transcended the suffering of seven million kalpas from beginning to end, and through the accumulation of a hundred thousand kalpas, he eliminated all karmic offenses and calamities. He beheld hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddhas from whom he received the roots of virtue, and for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, he served as Śakra, the Lord of Devas.

If one becomes a Brahmā or a Wheel-Turning Sage King, having accumulated merit and virtue, one governs all dharmas with a pure mind and will; with an undistracted mind, upon hearing of hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, one receives their teachings without forgetting them.
At that time, all the king’s sons attained the patient acceptance of the compliant Dharma (anulomikī-dharma-kṣānti);
the eighty-four thousand ladies of the inner palace universally resolved their minds on the Way and trained as bodhisattvas;
and eighty-four thousand people attained the patient acceptance of the Dharma.
Ninety nayutas of devas and humans all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path;
thirty-six nayutas who were training in the vehicle of the śrāvakas attained the purity of the Dharma-eye;
and ten thousand six thousand bhikṣus, with their outflows exhausted, attained liberation of mind.

“King Akṣayamati abandoned his kingdom and renounced his royal status; he did not long for the various pleasures of the heavens or the world, but set his mind solely upon the unsurpassed, true, and correct Way.
Relying on the faith of his household, he left the home life to practice the Way and became a śramaṇa.”
The princes did likewise, all becoming śramaṇas.
At that time, when the people of the country saw the king renounce his kingdom, sixty thousand people all became śramaṇas;
the ladies of the inner court, the palace attendants, and the four chief consorts also became śramaṇas.
"The Buddha-dharma is pure; all shall universally receive peace and security. They shall plant the roots of all virtues, and their manifold practices will be fully perfected.
The Buddha said, "O Dragon King!"
At that time, the Wheel-Turning Sage King, King Inexhaustible Merit, was none other than you yourself.
Those who were the sons of the Wheel-Turning Sage King at that time are these very Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas present in this assembly today.
The *Ratnavastu-dhāraṇī* which was taught by the Tathāgata Brahmaśirṣa-rāja for King Anantapuṇya is none other than this *Anantakośa-dhāraṇī* taught by the present Buddha.
The Buddha said to the Dragon King:

"Now the Tathāgata, observing the fundamental nature of beings with unattached wisdom, preaches the Dharma for them. Having heard from countless hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddhas the *dhāraṇī* of the inexhaustible treasury, it is because of having heard this so many times that he now possesses such resolute and courageous mindfulness, walks alone without obstruction, possesses eloquence difficult to equal, and harbors wisdom within his resolve."
If there are bodhisattvas who hear the name of this inexhaustible dhāraṇī, and whoever speaks of it, they shall all attain unimpeded eloquence. Why is this?
By means of this dhāraṇī, in future ages, wherever this stainless dhāraṇī is propagated, those places shall all be where the Tathāgata has established the eighty-four thousand treasuries of Dharma.

This gateway of dhāraṇī is the primary face; the eighty-four thousand practices all come to take refuge in the dhāraṇī, the eighty-four thousand samādhis all proceed from the dhāraṇī, and the inexhaustible treasury of the eighty-four thousand dhāraṇīs has the dhāraṇī as its fundamental source.
The Buddha said to the Dragon King:

"If a bodhisattva is without dwelling and without attachment, they will then pour down the great rain of Dharma upon the four modes of analytical understanding, and all shall come to rely upon this inexhaustible treasury."

This inexhaustible treasury of dhāraṇīs, with its sequential arrangement of verses and chapters, is protected by all the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, and kiṃnaras, who together maintain it:
"In accordance with conditions, following the intent and conforming to the will."
Delighting in the traces,
with a straightforward mind, one transcends.
The sequence of inexhaustible phrases illuminates the face.
The brilliance of his eyes and the excellence of his will were formed.
With pure conduct of mind, he enters with heroic strength.
That which is held by Jimit is supreme.
Entering the gate of tranquility to extinguish the dust of defilement.
Dwelling in seclusion, one dwells well in accordance with the Dharma.
Apart from the sequence,
there is no destination or place of abiding.
Non-abiding; reaching the place where there is no place to reach.
One must cultivate the faculty of wisdom characterized by swift intelligence.
The moonlight of the fundamental root revolves;
the sun revolves with blazing flames.
The light is virtuous, free from defilement, stainless,
and purifies all impurities.
The various deities established by awakening protect and guard against all malevolent spirits.
He addressed the Brahma-vehicle, informed the Śakras who know transformation, and uttered words of praise.
The Four Heavenly Kings protect the assembly; the sages beloved by the holy ones have returned.
Those of various lineages who practice the path and understand the bonds of the prison are embraced by devas and humans.
Abandoning all worldly defilements,
destroying the various māras,
and subduing the heterodox teachers.
To restrain desire, cultivate clear wisdom,
transform those who are arrogant,
and not transgress against the Dharma Master.
He does not disturb the assembly,
delights in the Dharma that brings joy,
and protects the sound of the Dharma.
"Sixty-two matters concerning not severing the Three Jewels, having compassion for sentient beings,
and praising and admiring virtuous conduct and righteousness. The Buddha told the Dragon King:
"These phrases of the Dharma constitute the dhāraṇī that protects the inexhaustible treasury.
Any Dharma Master who receives these sixty-two chapters and recites them shall attain the thirty-two grounds of fearlessness."
What are the thirty-two? They are:
possessing extensive learning and being fearless, praising others;
being fearless in all circumstances, and speaking without deficiency or fault.
Possessing fearlessness as appropriate, he casts off all solemnity;
being without fear, he enters into sounds according to their resonance;
with fearless eloquence, he is free from all obstruction.
His mind is fearless as he receives and upholds the aspiration for enlightenment;
his resolve is fearless as he brings joy to all people;
his conduct is fearless as he swiftly resolves all doubts.
The fearlessness of awakened mind, observing all beings;
the fearlessness of being without deficiency, where speech and action are in accord;
the fearlessness of being without flaw, with precepts and prohibitions purified.
Fearless in mind and countenance, with pure forbearance;
steadfast and fearless, not turning back from their profound vows;
fearless in whatever situation they dwell, their minds are neither deluded nor distracted.
Fearlessness in eloquence and wisdom can delight the assembled multitude;
fearlessness in wisdom knows the profound and subtle Dharma;
fearlessness in subduing and transforming is free from frivolous play.
With the fearlessness of a lion, he subdues all non-Buddhists;
with the fearlessness of being without acquisitions, he finds no pleasure in food or clothing;
with the fearlessness of being without blemish, he overcomes all bandits and causes them to abide in right view.
Being faultless and fearless, the wise do not disparage them;
guiding with fearlessness, they do not confuse the various sutras;
preaching with equanimity and fearlessness, they teach according to the occasion.
Free from flattery and fearless, their words and deeds correspond;
free from pride and fearless, they look upon all people;
humble and compliant and fearless, they cultivate the roots of goodness through inexhaustible phrases of fundamental practice.
The fearlessness of answering all inquiries, which opens and transforms all immeasurable teachings;
the fearlessness of conforming to the multitudes, because one’s own body is pure;
and the fearlessness of subduing Māra, which eliminates all worldly afflictions.
Great kindness and fearlessness, with a mind free from malice;
great compassion and fearlessness, protecting and sustaining all sentient beings;
wisdom and fearlessness, governing the state according to the Dharma.
The Buddha said to the Dragon King:
“When a bodhisattva hears this dhāraṇī of the inexhaustible treasury and rejoices with faith, they immediately attain the thirty-two forms of fearlessness.”
If one does not sever these thirty-two fearlessnesses, they will gradually and progressively become the Tathāgata’s four kinds of intrepidity—the intrepidities possessed by a Buddha.

Before the assembly of devas and humans, he let out a lion’s roar, inviting all to ask whatever they desired; yet no one was able to exhaustively fathom the Tathāgata’s wisdom, nor did anyone dare to interrupt what the Buddha spoke.
Therefore, a bodhisattva who wishes to attain these fearlessnesses should study and practice the dhāraṇī of the inexhaustible treasury.
What is this dhāraṇī that is to be studied and practiced?
There is no activity of the eye, no activity of forms, and no activity of eye-consciousness;
there is no activity of the ear, no activity of sounds, and no activity of ear-consciousness;
there is no activity of the nose, no activity of odors, and no activity of nose-consciousness.
There is no activity of the tongue, no activity of taste, and no activity of the consciousness of tongue and taste;
there is no activity of the body, no activity of tangibility, and no activity of the consciousness of body and tangibility;
there is no activity of the mind, no activity of phenomena, and no activity of the consciousness of mind and phenomena.
The practice of formlessness, the practice of the arising of formlessness, the practice of the cessation of formlessness, and the practice of the sphere of formlessness;

the practice of the absence of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, and the practice of the absence of the arising of consciousness, the practice of the absence of the cessation of consciousness, and the practice of the absence of the sphere of consciousness.
"All things are without activity; this is the practice that accords with the dhāraṇī.
Furthermore, O Dragon King!
To practice the emptiness of form while the mind does not empty form—this is the practice that accords with the dhāraṇī."

Regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness: since mental formations and consciousness are empty, yet the mind is not empty of consciousness, this is the practice corresponding to *dhāraṇī*.
Furthermore, regarding formless mental formations and not dwelling on those formless formations, this is the practice corresponding to *dhāraṇī*.

Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this: when there is no mental formation regarding perception and consciousness, and one does not even conceive of such a mental formation, this is the practice of dhāraṇī.

Furthermore, as for the practice of not interrupting form-activity: it is to practice no-activity regarding form-activity; it is to practice no-arising of form, no-origination of form, and no-quiescence of form; it is to practice the suchness of form and its original purity; yet, one does not even dwell on the mindfulness of the suchness and original purity of form. This is the practice of the dhāraṇī.

Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise. When one does not sever the activity of consciousness, yet there is no activity within the activity of consciousness; when one does not perceive the activity of arising, does not perceive the activity of origination, and does not perceive the activity of cessation; when one practices the truth of consciousness and practices the primordial purity of consciousness, yet does not even dwell upon the thought that consciousness is true or primordially pure—this is the practice of the dhāraṇī.

Furthermore, regarding the seeds, one practices through the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), yet does not conceive of practicing through the dharma-realm; one does not conceive of the fundamental purity and emptiness of the various entrances (āyatana) of the dharma-realm, nor does one conceive of that fundamental purity and emptiness. This is the practice of the dhāraṇī.
If one practices the dependent origination of all phenomena without conceptualizing dependent origination, this is the practice of dhāraṇī.
To practice without attachment to any phenomena, and to practice without reliance or clinging, is the practice of dhāraṇī.
All dharmas are, by their very nature, without activity; one does not destroy the original non-activity of all dharmas.

If one abides in the practice of the primordial limit regarding all dharmas, yet does not dwell on the thought of abiding in the primordial limit within the practice of all dharmas, this is the practice corresponding to dhāraṇī.
Furthermore, to know the practice of desire, yet not to conceive of the practice of desire within the dharma-realm—this is the practice corresponding to dhāraṇī.
To know the practice of hatred, yet not to conceive of the practice of hatred within the dharma-realm—this is the practice corresponding to dhāraṇī.
To know the conduct of delusion, yet not to harbor thoughts of delusion regarding the dharma-realm—this is the practice corresponding to dhāraṇī.
To have conduct of equal parts (*sabhāga*), yet not to harbor any thought of destroying the dharma-realm through such conduct of equal parts;
and if, among the eighty-four thousand modes of cultivation, one enters the dharma-realm without any thought of diversity—this is the practice corresponding to dhāraṇī.
Whether practicing alone or practicing in combination, one practices neither within the practice nor the combination, nor does one fail to practice. Why is this?
Because that practice is immeasurable and cannot be measured, and it is free from conceptualization; therefore, that practice is the practice of equality.

In the practice of equanimity, there is nothing to be disparaged; it is neither conditioned nor unconditioned, neither received nor unreceived, and being without location or abiding, it is therefore called the practice of equanimity.
"When a bodhisattva practices in this way, they attain the gate of the dhāraṇī of the inexhaustible treasury.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Their minds and intentions are pure, Universally entering the sūtras and attaining the *pāramitās*."
He fully understands the voices and languages of all people; such is his attainment of *dhāraṇī*.

Observing and knowing the mental activities of all living beings—their thoughts of good, evil, and that which lies between—he discerns the arising of their innate natures and speaks the Dharma for them according to what is appropriate.
Fully understanding the retribution of causes and conditions, they cause one not to perceive permanence or impermanence;
having abandoned all that falls into extremes, they distinguish the dhāraṇīs and transform others in accordance with them.
Clearly understanding the skillful means of written characters, knowing infinite sounds and resonances,
and thoroughly comprehending the subtle and wondrous meanings— such is one who has attained dhāraṇī.
Having attained the celestial eye, free from defilement, The celestial ear is likewise pure;
With immeasurable wisdom, he knows the conduct of all beings, And remembers the events of billions of kalpas past and future.
Attaining the four bases of spiritual power is likewise so:
in a mere moment, they reach immeasurable lands to make offerings to countless billions of Teachers, and having heard the Dharma they preach, they master it through dhāraṇī.
Even if many hundreds of thousands of millions of Māras were to arrive, they could not perceive the conduct within his sphere;
this pure person, free from all dust, expounds the Dharma in countless thousands of ways.
Just as a lotus flower is unstained by water, so too does one not rely upon worldly dharmas;
always liberated from all states of existence, one regards all things with a mind equal to space.
Bearing the most excellent physical marks with heroic vigor, all people look up to him without ever wearying;
his movements are serene and composed, his conduct flawless, for he wanders through the world out of compassion for all living beings.
Śakra, Brahmā, and the World-Protectors all pay homage with reverence;
their minds do not speak out of arrogance—when one attains dhāraṇī, it is also thus.
His speech is soft and supple like the voice of Brahmā; he speaks for the sake of the multitude in a way that accords with their hearts.
His words are warm, smooth, and fluent, spoken at the proper time; those whom he seeks to transform are never left unrevealed.
Amidst the multitude, they are fearless; They roar the lion’s roar with wondrous ease, Subduing all coarse and vulgar people; Thus do they attain the pure dhāraṇī.
Those who are flatterers and difficult to transform, who give rise to arrogance and self-importance,
upon hearing the Dharma taught by that Sage of Supreme Clarity, immediately cast aside their haughtiness and prostrate themselves in worship.
Entering the fundamentally pure and quiescent dharma-realm, one attains the ultimate meaning and realizes all phenomena;
thus, what is taught is inexhaustible, as one discerns words and understands the Dharma and Vinaya.
The nature of human beings is the purity of the Dharma-realm; They understand that the purity of sentient beings is likewise so.
Knowing that fundamentally there is no person and that the person is originally non-existent, The sūtra-dharmas they preach are without hindrance.
That which is exhausted is unknowable as being inexhaustible; that which is inexhaustible cannot be exhausted.
To awaken to and know this as the path to stillness, one then preaches billions of scrolls of non-abiding sutras.
These written characters do not abide in the body, nor do they reside in the intellect or dwell in the mind;
the intrinsic nature of characters is empty and silent, like an echo from a shout in the mountains.
One who masters the dhāraṇīs does not cling to letters; there is no sound, no speech, and no vocalized expression.
Because they know the nature of how characters function, whatever they may say is without obstruction.
Without volition, without perception, and without mind, even when there is something spoken, there is no conceptualization;
furthermore, understanding the wisdom of the dharma of departure, one preaches the sutras in accordance with what is appropriate.
By entering into the analysis of the fourfold logic, he thoroughly understands the principles and clearly discerns all phenomena;
having mastered sounds and speech according to what is heard, he thus preaches with non-attachment in an immeasurable way.
By practicing and studying the fundamental source, one receives its wisdom; thus, various profound and essential dharmas are taught.
Through the wisdom of understanding that which is resolved, one penetrates both the adverse and the favorable; this is the *śīla-śikhara-dhāraṇī-pāramitā*.
Using skillful means to gather in all who are timid and weak, and employing them to restrain those who are impulsive and violent;
clearly discerning what should be done and providing explanations—such is the one who has attained dhāraṇī.
His body, speech, and mind are all already stilled; he discerns various wisdoms without clinging to the past.
His words are never wearying as he eliminates anger and resentment, attaining the dhāraṇī and becoming courageous.
That which his mind maintains through total retention and governs, and the wisdom of the Dharma in which his intent dwells—those who hear it never forget it;
they accord with it as if listening to and collecting the various sūtras.
The meaning of its dhāraṇī is that phenomena are not disordered; calculating the practice of phenomena, there is nowhere to enter.
Because phenomena are equal, they are called "equality"; as they accord with this equality, they conform to purity.

8. Chapter on the Analysis of Names (2). When the Buddha spoke these verses and phrases, thirteen thousand dragons from the retinue of Sāgara, the Dragon King, all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, perfect, and true path, and they further addressed him, saying:
"Please proclaim this teaching extensively; so be it, World-Honored One!"
"We, too, shall attain this dhāraṇī of the inexhaustible treasury and shall extensively expound the Dharma for the sake of all classes of sentient beings!
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is truly unprecedented!
“World-Honored One!
You have caused these dragons to resolve upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path, yet humans, on the contrary, are unable to resolve upon the Great Way!
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"These thirteen thousand dragons were all śramaṇas during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha; having heard the bodhisattva practice once from the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, they simultaneously rejoiced and praised, saying:
'Excellent, excellent!'"
"It is inconceivable that you should speak of the matters of the Mahāyāna!

Together with his kinsmen and friends, he went out to beg for alms; yet, being greedy for gain and lacking self-restraint, he failed to guard the prohibitive precepts. For this reason, after his life ended, he fell among the dragons.

At that time, having heard the Mahāyāna teachings from Kāśyapa Buddha and praised him, they now hear my discourse on the Mahāyāna due to the conditions of their karmic retribution and roots of virtue; as I expound the *dhāraṇī* of the inexhaustible treasury, they all resolve to attain unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment.

Śāriputra! Behold the extraordinary nature of this supreme sincerity. Now I bestow upon them their prediction: for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, they shall make offerings to various Buddhas and accumulate the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*), until they themselves attain the realization of the unsurpassed, right, and true path. They shall be named Hui-shang (Supreme Wisdom), Zhi-shang (Supreme Knowledge), Fa-shang (Supreme Dharma), and Fan-shang (Supreme Brahma). When they attain Buddhahood, because of these four matters, their world shall be named Wu-gou-zang (Stainless Treasury), and the kalpa shall be named Da-xin (Great Joy); all shall together, within that same single kalpa, attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path of supreme perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), just as in the Bhadrakalpa, when one thousand Buddhas are destined to arise.
Chapter Nine: Bestowing Prophecy (2) At that time, the Dragon King Sāgara addressed the Buddha, saying:

“Since I first dwelt in the great ocean at the beginning of the kalpa, from the time the Tathāgata Krakucchanda appeared in the world until now, the number of dragon wives, children, and retinues within the great ocean was very small. Now, the descendants of the dragon hosts—wives, children, and retinues—are vast and numerous; were one to attempt to calculate them, they could not be exhausted.”
"So be it, World-Honored One!
How is it that such a portentous anomaly has occurred?
The Buddha told the Dragon King:

“Those who have gone forth in the Buddha’s Dharma, upholding the discipline and practicing the precepts, yet fail to fully manifest the perfection of the precepts and instead violate them through transgressive conduct—provided they do not abandon right view—they shall not fall into hell.”
"Beings of such a kind, after their lives have ended, are all reborn among the dragons.
The Buddha said to the Dragon King:
"During the time of Krakucchanda Buddha, nine billion eight hundred million householders and renunciants violated the prohibitions and precepts, and were all reborn among the dragons."

During the time of the Buddha Kanakamuni, eight billion householders and renunciants violated the precepts and gave rein to their desires; after their lives ended, they were all reborn among the nāgas.
During the time of the Buddha Kāśyapa, six billion four hundred million householders and renunciants broke the precepts; after their lives ended, they were all reborn among the nāgas.

Within my world, nine hundred and ninety billion householders and renunciants engaged in various disputes and practiced various conducts; they slandered the sūtras and the precepts, and after their lives ended, they were all reborn among the nāgas—some of whom are still living there today.
The Buddha said to the Dragon King:
"For this reason, O Benevolent One, the wives, children, and retinues of the various dragons within the great ocean are beyond calculation.
After my parinirvāṇa, there will be many wicked bhikṣus and wicked upāsakas who violate and lose the prohibitive precepts; they shall be reborn among the dragons or fall into the hells."
The Dragon King Sāgara addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Regarding those who have now left home to practice the Way, what is so extraordinary about a bhikṣu who falls among the dragons due to violating the precepts?"
The Buddha said:

"Regarding those who have left home to study and practice, yet now fall among the dragons as monks who have violated the precepts—it is because they failed to practice skillful means and could not maintain purity."

Furthermore, there are those who possess a mind of supreme faith in the Buddha-dharma; by the power of that supreme mind, they pass away from among the dragons and are reborn in the heavens or the human realm, where they shall behold all the Buddhas who arise during the Bhadrakalpa. They shall indeed see them all.
Even if they were not yet liberated, they would all enter parinirvāṇa during the Bhadrakalpa, with the exception of those whose resolve was set upon the Mahāyāna.
O Dragon King!

Behold the vast causes and conditions of the Buddha’s teaching, and the extraordinary nature of going forth from home: by abandoning all unwholesome dharmas, one attains transcendence beyond the various classes of beings.
At that time, there was a dragon prince named Virasheṣa, who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is truly unprecedented,
World-Honored One!"

The Dragon King is near to the Tathāgata; he is difficult to encounter and difficult to hear. Although he has committed destructions and wrought many sinful calamities, if he gives rise to even a single thought of wholesome intent and brings the Buddha-Dharma to mind, he will ultimately not lose his virtue;
by means of this practice, he shall attain nirvāṇa.

Now I vow to give rise to the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment. Since a Buddha, a World-Honored One, is difficult to encounter and difficult to hear, I shall ensure that my bodhisattva practice remains free from violation or deficiency until I reach the site of enlightenment. May I never forget the roots of virtue within my mind; with great kindness, great compassion, great joy, and great protection, may I always see the Buddhas in every place where I am born, hear the Dharma, make offerings to the Sangha, and transform sentient beings.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Dragon Prince Viśeṣamati, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! Your inquiry has arisen from a mind intent upon the salvation and protection of all beings."

Now that you have, with a sincere heart, aroused boundless compassion and resolved upon the path, the Tathāgata praises this root of virtue; for seven days, seven months, or even up to a year, the merit and blessings thereof shall be inexhaustible—such indeed is the nature of the wholesome deeds you have planted!
The Buddha, perceiving the thoughts in the mind of the dragon prince Viśeṣamati, immediately smiled with joy.

According to the law of the Buddhas' smiles, immeasurable colors emerged, each distinct from the others; light issued from his mouth, illuminating incalculable Buddha-worlds, circled his body three times, and returned to enter through the crown of his head.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda praised the Buddha in verse:
“Your body is adorned with the merit of a hundred blessings, Possessing all thirty-two marks of excellence;
Pure and stainless like the light of the moon— What inspires this smile of yours today?”
Tranquil, free from dust, and devoid of the three impurities, Like a hundred-petaled lotus, you act without weariness;
Honored and revered by devas, humans, nāgas, and spirits— Abiding thus in peace, for what reason do you smile?
Excellent are your even teeth, universally pure; your face, radiant with the majesty of the Ten Powers, is fragrant and clean.
Having eradicated the very root of birth and death, for what reason, World-Honored One, do you smile now?
The mind is like space, free from blemish; the will is equal toward both good friends and enemies;
one’s resolve is like the earth, without hatred or love. I pray only that the World-Honored One tell me: for what reason do you smile?
The sounds he utters are like those of Brahmā, Resonant as thunder and as subtle as the cry of a phoenix;
His speech is so gentle that all rejoice— We pray only that the World-Honored One will explain the causes and conditions.

The mind is unattached to noble wisdom; knowing the mental activities of beings in the three periods of time, and understanding the faculties of the multitude to attain joy—O Guide, for what reason do you now smile?
Thinking that he has become a King of Physicians, who cures the diseases of all beings and can bestow ultimate peace—O World-Honored One, for what reason do you smile?
O Protector of Virtue, tell me this; may the devas and the people hear it.
"All should harbor joy and exultation, and immediately set their minds upon the various supernormal powers and wisdom.
The Buddha said to the venerable Ānanda:
"Do you see the Dragon Prince Viśeṣamati standing before the Buddha, with a sincere mind resolving to attain the unsurpassed, true, and right path?"
Ānanda replied, "Indeed, I have seen it. The Buddha said:

"This Dragon Prince Viśeṣamati, after passing through eight hundred incalculable, immeasurable, and infinite kalpas, shall attain Buddhahood; his name shall be Jñānadarśana Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. His world shall be named Viśuddhavihāra, and the kalpa shall be called Vipaśyanā."

This Prince of the Dragon Nāgas sincerely practiced the path of the Bodhisattva; he beheld countless Tathāgatas, made offerings to and served them, constantly cultivated the pure conduct (brahmacarya), and transformed and liberated immeasurable sentient beings, establishing them in the Three Vehicles.

The Tathāgata Prajñādṛśya’s world, Pure Abode (Viśuddhasthiti), is abundant, prosperous, peaceful, and secure; the five grains are plentiful and inexpensive, its bliss is immeasurable, and it is filled with devas and humans, whose clothing and food are like those of the Yāma Heaven.
That Buddha’s lifespan shall be one million years; his assembly of noble and holy monks consisting of śrāvakas shall number sixty billion, and his bodhisattvas one hundred and twenty trillion.
Any who behold that Tathāgata Prajñādṛśa shall all attain the Samādhi of Compassionate Conduct.
In the sūtras spoken by the Tathāgata, it is said that for a practitioner of the Śrāvaka vehicle, if they see the Buddha for the first time, they attain the fruit of Stream-entry;
seeing him a second time, they attain the fruit of Once-returning; and seeing him a third time, they attain the fruit of Non-returning.
Regarding the four views, they attain non-attachment.
Those who resolve upon the Bodhisattva vehicle, upon first beholding the Tathāgata Prajñādṛśa, attain the patience of compliance;
upon seeing him a second time, they obtain the supernormal powers.
Through the third vision, one attains dhāraṇī and eloquence;
through the fourth vision, one attains the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
In this world of Pure Abiding, there are none who violate the precepts; their minds are pure and free from deviance, and all abide in right view.
"After the end of their lives, they shall have no rebirth in the evil realms, but shall all be born in the pure Buddha-fields of the heavens.

At that time, having heard the Buddha bestow this prophecy, the dragon prince Viśeṣamati was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; a virtuous mind arose within him, and he offered a necklace of hundreds of thousands of pearls, scattering it over the Buddha. With his ten fingers joined in prayer, he praised him in verse:
"The Honored One among Men is stainless like the moonlight; His majestic power is immeasurable, and he is venerated by the multitudes."
His power is infinite, he sustains the world; I vow to bow my head in worship to him of boundless wisdom.
The Sage of compassion is beyond limit; his brilliant wisdom is flawless and beyond discourse.
His prohibitions and precepts are vast and universal, and he abides in right concentration; I bow my head to the Honored One among Men, who is like space.
Throughout immeasurable and limitless billions of kalpas, there is nothing he has not mastered through his ultimate practice;
therefore, he clearly understands the fundamental nature of all sentient beings and where their minds ultimately return.
If one beholds the countenance of the Honored One, observing it with single-mindedness without weariness,
they will not be deluded by the dust of the world, and the defilements of craving and desire will all be extinguished.
The cries of the mourning pheasant and the various spirits of Kuyi, and even the voice of Brahmā, are likewise [limited];
though their sounds reach the ten directions with great subtlety, the Tathāgata’s voice transcends them all.
It would be as if the sun were to fall to the earth, the waters of the ocean were to dry up, Mount Sumeru were to crumble, the void were to split asunder, and the earth were to turn upside down;
yet that which the World-Honored One has spoken shall never be otherwise.
The World-Honored One has spoken with utmost sincerity and truth, bestowing upon me the distinguished great wisdom of the Sage;
my doubts are gone and the web of fetters removed, and I have attained the sovereignty of a Buddha to become a protector for all beings.
Even if one were to fill the immeasurable billions of lands throughout the ten directions with precious jewels as an offering to the Teacher,
if another person were to give rise to the mind of enlightenment, the merit previously planted would not equal this.
Making offerings to the Perfectly Awakened One, whose virtue is supreme— if a person resolves to attain the honored path of the Buddha,
they thereby repay the kindness of those possessed of the ten powers and sustain the life of this Teacher without interruption.
After the Dragon Prince had spoken these verses in praise of the Buddha, ten thousand people all resolved to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment, and they all said:

“When the Tathāgata Prajñādṛśya attains supreme, perfect awakening, we shall together with one mind be born in the world Pure Abode (Śuddhāvāsa), where we shall uphold the teachings of that Tathāgata’s True Dharma and make offerings to him.”
"After the Buddha's parinirvāṇa, they shall succeed him in his place and attain supreme perfect enlightenment.
The Buddha bestowed this prediction upon them all, decreeing that they shall all be born in the world-system of Pure Abode.
The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Naga King Sagara, Volume II;
The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Naga King Sagara, Volume III.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Yuezhi Kingdom during the Western Jin Dynasty.
10. Chapter on Inviting the Buddha (3). Chapter Ten: Inviting the Buddha.
At that time, the Dragon King Sāgara addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

"May the Buddha, out of compassion for the devas, nāgas, spirits, and immeasurable humans, grant them peace and security as they reach the great ocean; I pray that you will deign to visit my palace and partake of a small meal."

Why is this? Within the great ocean there are dragons, spirits, gandharvas, and countless other species of sentient beings; having seen the Tathāgata, they shall all plant the roots of virtue and gather at this assembly, whereby, through hearing the sound of the Dharma, they will sever the bottomless source of birth and death.

We, the dragons of our palace, have likewise received his grace; through the conditions of the heavens and the world, we have attained liberation. The Tathāgata universally manifests the Great Bodhicitta of the Buddha, enabling us to draw near to the dharmas of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma).
The Buddha, out of compassion for the Dragon King, silently accepted his invitation; he also intended that immeasurable people should all extensively cultivate the roots of manifold virtues.

At that time, seeing that the Buddha had accepted his invitation, the Sea Dragon King leaped for joy; he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and together with his retinue, suddenly vanished from sight.
Returning once more to the great ocean, he gathered the dragon people together and addressed them, saying:
"I have invited the Buddha for tomorrow, and the Buddha has graciously granted his consent; you all, with one heart, should provide offerings together."
The Dragon King Sāgara further addressed the devas Kāyasthita-aśubha, Vañcana-bandhana, and Vimala-kauśeya, saying:
"O virtuous ones, you should know that the Tathāgata has sent forth his spirit; he shall come to this ocean!"
"It is fitting that you come in person, leading your retinues to assemble at my palace to present food offerings to the World-Honored One.

He further commanded the dragon kings named King Sovereign Deliverance, King Praising the Immeasurable, King Free from Defilement, King Blazing Light, King Sporting Joy, King Pure, King Sublime Radiant Mind, and King Manifesting All Difficulties, along with a multitude of hundreds of thousands of other dragon kings, saying: "All of you shall gather at my palace to pay your respects to the Tathāgata."
He further commanded the dragon prince Wei-shou, saying:
"O Benevolent One!
Pay your respects and proclaim my command to the Dragon King Wu-fen, ordering all the palaces of the ocean to make offerings to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha."
He immediately accepted the instruction.

Furthermore, he commanded the dragon prince Vīrabala to go to the summit of Mount Anomā to invite the Dragon King Nanda, the Dragon King Upananda, and Śakra, Lord of Devas, commanding these worthy ones to proceed to the great ocean and assemble within my palace to make offerings to the Tathāgata.
Then, upon receiving these instructions, Bhīṣmottaranirghoṣa issued such a proclamation.

At that time, the Dragon King Sāgara manifested a great palace, constructed from a mixture of deep-blue lapis lazuli and purple-golden refined gold. He erected banners and streamers and fashioned golden lattices; with precious pearls, necklaces, and the seven treasures, he formed railings that were exceedingly vast. It was perfumed with various kinds of incense, and flowers of many colors were scattered about, falling like snow.

Within the great hall, he miraculously established a lion throne four hundred and eighty li high, composed entirely of various precious jewels, upon which were spread countless hundreds of thousands of celestial silks as carpets and hangings.
The lion seats upon which the various bodhisattvas and the assembly of bhikṣus sat were each magnificent and resplendent, with distinct tiers and levels.
The provisions were doubly abundant, consisting of various flavors; they partook of the food and drink in silence, as all the offerings had been fully prepared.

At that time, early on the following morning, the Dragon King performed his respects and, staying at the twelfth cave of Mount Anoma, together with his retinue, invited the World-Honored One from afar, speaking in verse:
"Your extraordinary wisdom is immeasurable; You have attained mastery over all phenomena.
With clear knowledge you accomplish all deeds, Like the infinite space of the sages."
With eyes pure and free from defilement, you are the most supreme in the world;
the time has now arrived—please deign to show compassion and humble yourself.
Your pure voice is like that of Brahmā; your gentle sound is harmonious and benevolent.
The resonance of his thunder is like the cry of the sorrowful phoenix; for the sake of the multitude, he manifests the nectar of immortality.
He dispels manifold dust and darkness, serving as the supreme physician for all beings.
O Jewel among Men, we pray that you will come; now is truly the time.
With a mind that is pliant, tranquil, and serene, And a will that is gentle, ever peaceful, and harmonious; Having crossed over oneself,
one delivers all sentient beings, Vowing to rescue the masses of people,
To enlighten and transform the common folk, Causing them to transcend those four great rivers.
Having built the bridge to the further shore, now is indeed the time for you to bend [to our request].
You who delight in benevolence and practice giving, who study the Way with pure precepts,
whose power of patience is supreme, and who have already attained great diligence—
Having extinguished the meditative absorptions and liberations, his wisdom is universally immeasurable;
his spoken instructions are as bright as the moon. The time has come for him to abide in the state of the Noble Ones.
The tracks of wisdom now diverge onto separate paths, and the wrong ways have been forever severed.
With the seven factors of enlightenment, the faculties, and the powers, you manifest through the Four Truths;
with the four foundations of mindfulness and the four bases of psychic power, you have attained universal penetration.
Now that the time has come, it is fitting that you bend your divine will to appear.
The thirty-two marks are radiant; with a hundred wondrous merits, he manifests as a great field of merit for those who preserve virtue and righteousness.
Honored as the Protector of the Multitudes, he flourishes like sprouts in spring.
Out of pure compassion, you bestow kindness; out of great pity, you humble yourself.
Your will is like Mount Sumeru, and your mind is as even as the earth.
Having eliminated the darkness of craving and hatred, your teaching unfolds like the exposition of emptiness.
The Honored One among Men does not humble himself, nor has he ever been arrogant;
having entered the gate of emptiness and liberation, he now bends his spirit for this very moment.
Knowing the meaning, he discerns it immediately; he clearly understands and accords with the essential principles.
Thoroughly elucidating the methods of the scriptures, with a mind and conduct always like this,
revealing the fundamental nature of beings and contemplating the meaning of all wisdoms—
I bow my head to the feet of the Most Victorious One; the time has come, please deign to descend.
At that time, the World-Honored One heard from afar the Dragon King’s announcement that the time had arrived, and he addressed the bhikṣus:
"Put on your robes and take up your bowls; we shall go to the great ocean to transform sentient beings and partake of a meal at the dragon palace."
The bhikṣu replied, “So be it!

Thereupon, the World-Honored One, together with the assembly of bodhisattvas and the community of bhikṣus, surrounded by his retinue, leaped into the air. His body emitted a great radiance, and celestial flowers rained down; hundreds of thousands of musical instruments played in harmonious concert as they gathered at the seashore and arrived at the Garden of Joy.
There was a campaka flower named Manojña (Intention-Delight), and the Buddha was dwelling there.
At that time, the Naga King Sāgara went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and having finished his respectful salutation, withdrew to stand to one side.
The Dragon King thought to himself:

"I wish to manifest jeweled stairways extending from the seashore to the bottom of the ocean, so that the Buddha, the assembly of bhikṣus, and the various bodhisattvas may descend by them into the ocean and reach my palace—just as in the past the World-Honored One manifested jeweled stairways descending from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to Jambudvīpa."

As soon as this thought arose, three stairways made of the Three Jewels—gold, silver, and lapis lazuli—were miraculously manifested from the seashore, extending down to her palace, which was exceedingly subtle and exquisite.

Thereupon, by means of his majestic spiritual power, the World-Honored One transformed the waters of the great ocean so that they no longer appeared, ensuring that the creatures dwelling in the sea would not suffer distress.
From his body, the Buddha emitted light that illuminated the great ocean and reached throughout the entire trichiliocosm.

When the beings dwelling in that ocean were bathed by this light, they all conceived hearts of compassion, kindness, gentleness, and benevolence; they no longer harmed one another, regarding each other as fathers, mothers, elder brothers, younger brothers, or sons, without any difference.

At that time, the devas of the realm of desire and the devas of the realm of form attended upon the World-Honored One, desiring to hear his transformation through the Way, just as they wished to behold the magnificent palace adorned by the Dragon King.

At that time, the Buddha, together with the bodhisattvas, the great śrāvakas, and the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, Śakra, Brahmā, and the four heavenly kings, departed from the tree of *campaka* flowers in the Garden of Joy (*Nandana-vana*) intending to go to the dragon palace.
The Buddha ascended the jeweled stairs and proceeded along the central flight.
The assembly of bodhisattvas stood upon the right flight, while the great śrāvakas stood upon the left flight.
At that time, six billion Śakras led the way in front.
Six billion Brahmā devas were all in the air, each holding a precious parasol;
six billion devas were all behind the Buddha, raining down celestial flowers;
and six billion devas of the desire realm performed various musical performances as an offering to the Buddha.
Six billion hosts of Māras all sprinkled fragrant liquid upon the ground before the Buddha;
six billion dragon queens remained in the void, each manifesting half a body with hands holding strings of pearls and jewels which they scattered down over the Buddha;
and six billion mountain deities all played musical instruments and sang praises of the Buddha’s virtues.
Six billion gandharva deities held flower canopies in their hands to offer to the Buddha;
six billion asura deities each held hundreds of thousands of varieties of garments to drape over the Buddha;

and the Dragon King Anala, together with his hundreds of thousands of millions of retinues, remained in the void, all using flowers, incense, blended perfumes, and powdered incense, performing various musical offerings, adorning themselves as dragons, and presenting celestial flowers to make offerings to the Buddha.
In this manner, sixty thousand dragon kings all made offerings to the Buddha, desiring to see the World-Honored One and encouraging the Dragon King Sāgara.

Bodhisattvas from the land of the Tathāgata Amitāyus in the world Sukhāvatī—namely the Mahāsattvas Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta—along with countless billions of other bodhisattvas, manifested for the Buddha, the World-Honored One, a magnificent array of all manner of offerings. These completely eclipsed all the previously prepared offerings so that no one could perceive them.
In the world-system Jvālā, in the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Durlabha, there are bodhisattvas known as Dharmakīrti and Dharmamārga Mahāsattvas;
in the world-system Sukhāvatī, in the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Akṣobhya, there are bodhisattvas known as Gandhamukha and Gandharāja Mahāsattvas;
in the world-system Avabhāsana, in the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Candravikrama, there are bodhisattvas known as Siṃha and Siṃhasvara Mahāsattvas.
The bodhisattvas from the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Sunetra in the world Animiṣā are known as the Great Beings Ācārya and Dharmeśvara;
the bodhisattvas from the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Viśvabhū in the world Prabhāsa are known as the Great Beings Ratnavyūha and Ratnajvāla;
the bodhisattvas from the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Ratnaśrī in the world Sukhācāra are known as the Great Beings Jñānakrama and Jñānadarśana.
In the world Radiant Observation, there is a bodhisattva in the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Universal Observer named Rain King, the Great Being of the Dharma King;
in the world Beloved Vision, there is a bodhisattva in the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Sovereign Lord of Freedom named Vanquisher of Māra, the Great Being of the Māra King.

To speak briefly, in this manner, countless billions of bodhisattvas from each of the ten directions have all come to encourage and delight the Dragon King of the Ocean Sea, desiring to see the Tathāgata and to make offerings and serve him.

Thereupon, the World-Honored One, by the power of the Great Way and the resonance of all Buddhas, under the surveillance of his majestic virtue, and through the Buddha’s vast majesty, exhorted and transformed beings without frivolity; he made offerings to all Buddhas and emitted a great radiance that thoroughly illuminated immeasurable worlds throughout the ten directions. With the Buddha’s profound voice, like the great lion’s roar, he preached the Dharma to transform hundreds of thousands of devas; they all played music and rained down celestial flowers, extinguishing all evil realms and bestowing upon all beings the requisites for peace and security.

There is a samādhi called "Abiding in Great Compassion and Gladdening All Sentient Beings"; having entered this Buddha-samādhi through meditative absorption, the magnificent adornments and radiant embellishments he manifests are inconceivable, like a great ocean.
As the Buddha descended from the jeweled stairs into the ocean palace, celestial music spontaneously resounded throughout immeasurable worlds in the ten directions.
Through the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata and his miraculous influence, all beheld the Tathāgata Śākyamuni descending into the great ocean.

At that time, hundreds of thousands of millions of jade maidens, wives of Māra, as well as *asura* goddesses, *garuḍa* goddesses, mountain goddesses, *apsaras* goddesses, and the wives of various deities, all came forth to welcome the Buddha with music. They tuned their instruments and sang in praise of the Buddha’s virtues:

"Bestower of supreme precepts and purity, Honored One whose power is patience and whose heart is compassion, Diligent in the meaning of energetic self-mastery, Master of ritual, music, meditation, and the gates of liberation."
With the wisdom of pure mental radiance, adorned with brilliance and manifesting majestic spiritual power, you now demonstrate liberation; thus you have come to remove defilements and dust.
Bestowing the peace of ambrosia, you drive away all impurities through the governance of the Path.
Inexhaustible virtue like space, the ocean of wisdom—may you descend upon this sea!
Your teachings are complete in their essentials; your exposition and praise constitute the *pāramitā* of deliverance.
Bestowing the eye of clear and pure vision, you are the supreme among all people.
Chanting verses on the profound meaning, his light for the sake of humanity is peerless;
he proclaims universally from the altar of equanimity, subduing all heterodox paths.
Bestowing the Dharma without stinginess, he preaches the sutras to purify and dispel the dust of afflictions.
I praise the light of true wisdom, the precious unfolding of the wealth of the Path.
Those who see the Truth cannot fail to receive it; through right contemplation, they sever all fetters and attachments.
Unshakable as the roots of a mountain, I vow to bow my head before the Teacher.
The devas, garuḍas, asuras, kinnaras, and mahoragas— may they all prostrate at your feet.
Your thirty-two marks of excellence appear most wondrous and peerless.
Your body is supple and of purple-gold hue; your nails and the soles of your feet are level and even.

Your wondrous resonance is like that of the mourning pheasant; your voice surpasses that of the Brahma heavens and your great sound transcends the trichiliocosm. I bow my head to you of the soft and gentle voice.
With faculties subdued and mind tranquil, like the moon or a flash of lightning, your speech is truthful and ever-equal; I prostrate to you who delight in the Dharma.
Having transcended the suffering of old age and illness, you rescue all beings and bring them to liberation.
Having attained victory over all Māras, he extinguishes birth and brings existence to an end.
Unattached and free from worldly toil, he is revered by the devas;
taking refuge in the Honored One who universally protects, the Teacher transforms and enlightens the multitudes.

11. Chapter Eleven: The Ten Virtues and the Six Perfections.
