At that time, the princess, along with the various dragon queens, the *asura* goddesses, the *garuḍa* goddesses, the mountain deities, and the goddesses of the sweet and gentle realms, having together praised the Buddha, all equally resolved their minds toward unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), and they removed the necklaces from their bodies to scatter them over the Buddha.

The Buddha, together with the assembly, descended to the great ocean. Upon reaching the city on the sea, he proceeded to the magnificently adorned great hall of the Sea Dragon King and sat upon the lion throne.
At that time, the various bodhisattvas and the assembly of bhikṣus each sat in their respective seats in order.

At that time, the Dragon King Sāgara, together with his queens and retinue, having seen the Buddha seated, personally served and offered food and drink in silence; they provided the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus with offerings of countless flavors.

When the meal was finished and the ritual washing of hands had been completed, they sat before the Buddha to listen to the sutra, together with the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, mountain deities, kinnaras, Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Heavenly Kings, and the bodhisattvas who had gathered from the ten directions.
Thereupon, the Buddha, seeing that the assembly was seated, emitted light from his body; this light, named "Gentle and Soft Dharma of Excellent Deliverance," illuminated the entire great ocean.

All beings dwelling therein—of superior, middling, and inferior grades—universally beheld the Buddha for themselves. Overjoyed and leaping with delight, they yearned to hear the Dharma and each, with reverence, bowed their heads from afar toward the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Dragon King Sāgara:

"Those who rely upon the world create various conditions; their mental activities differ, and their offenses and blessings vary accordingly. For this reason, those born [into different realms] are distinct from one another."
"O Dragon King!
Behold this assembly and the great ocean with their various kinds of forms and appearances; all these forms and appearances are painted by the mind.

Furthermore, the mind has no form and cannot be seen. All phenomena are deceptive in this way: they arise through conditions and possess no master, yet each receives its own retribution according to what it has done."
For example, a painter originally has no created image; all phenomena are likewise inconceivable, naturally like the appearance of illusions and transformations, all produced by the mind.
"Clarity" means that when one perceives the causes of all phenomena or their arising characteristics, one should then practice all forms of goodness.

"Virtue" means that when one understands how the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense bases (*āyatana*) arise and are established as all phenomena, one should feel joyful gladness and attain a state of sublime excellence.
"O Dragon King!

Behold the body of the Tathāgata: it is composed of hundreds of thousands of merits and transcends all assemblies, appearing everywhere with majestic sublimity. By virtue of these hundreds of thousands of virtues, he attains sovereign mastery, such that even Brahmā and Śakra are eclipsed and do not appear."

Beholding the body of the Tathāgata, one dares not gaze upon it; yet when one examines the various Great Beings under his majestic radiance, their physical forms and marks of excellence are fully adorned, for they have all embellished their bodies with virtuous merit.
The Buddha said to the Dragon King:
"That which you have so solemnly purified is all accomplished through merit.
All the adornments of the Śakras, Brahmās, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, mountain deities, and sweet-voiced deities arise from merit."

Now, within this great ocean, there are various kinds of bodies—good or evil, large or small, broad or narrow, beautiful or ugly, strong or weak, subtle or minute—all of which are obtained solely from the mind and manifest as various forms; they are entirely the products of the actions of body, speech, and mind.
Therefore, O Dragon King!
You should train yourselves in this way: protect your own physical conduct and rescue yourselves from both demerit and merit.

By protecting your physical conduct and rescuing yourselves from demerit and merit, you shall practice all forms of goodness, attain the Buddha-way, and cast off false views. Abiding neither in the view of permanence nor in the view of impermanence, you should seek the protection of the multitudes and plant the seeds of offerings.
"Because of this offering, you shall be revered by all devas and worldly beings!
The Buddha said to the Dragon King:
"A Bodhisattva possesses one dharma that completely severs all evil destinies and manifold hardships."
What is this one thing?
It is to single-mindedly examine the sublime Dharma: what constitutes the correct truths?
One enters into the joy of the Dharma, frequently contemplates wholesome dharmas, and does not listen to various evil or heterodox thoughts.
"Having severed unwholesome dharmas and practiced all manner of virtues,
wherever they are born, they shall be accompanied by Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and those of virtuous nature.
The Buddha said:
"What is this wholesome deed that establishes the roots of virtue for the peace of devas and humans, yet does not become the basis for the stage of Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas?
To establish the foundation of the Way is to set one's will upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path."
What is meant by "establishing the foundation"?
It refers to practicing ten matters. What are these ten?

Not killing, stealing, or engaging in sexual misconduct with the body; not speaking falsely, divisively, harshly, or frivolously with the mouth; and not harboring envy, malice, or delusion with the mind—this is called establishing the foundation.
The Buddha said to the Dragon King:
"If a person refrains from killing, they attain the ten wholesome dharmas of tranquility.
What are these ten?"

They constantly bestow peace and security upon all people and always delight in a mind of loving-kindness, severing all thoughts of anger and resentment. Wherever they are born, they are forever free from illness; they constantly plant the seeds of long life and are protected by non-human beings. They sleep in peace and awaken with joy, never experiencing bad dreams. Free from harboring grudges, they do not fear the evil realms, and after their lives end, they attain rebirth in a place of peace.
By refraining from killing, a person attains this tranquil Dharma; through the merit of the wholesome root of non-killing, they vow their aspiration for the unsurpassed, true, and correct path.
When they attain Buddhahood, they shall obtain mastery over their lifespan.
The Buddha told the Dragon King:
"A person who does not steal obtains five dharmas of faith.
What are these five?"

One will attain great wealth that cannot be stolen by government officials, water, fire, thieves, enemies, or wicked sons; one will be loved and respected by all, remaining tranquil wherever one goes, meeting with no obstacles, and having all suffering and fear forever eliminated.

By virtue of the merit of non-grasping and with a mind intent on wise giving, they plant the roots of manifold virtues and aspire to the unsurpassed, right, and true Way. Relying upon the Tathāgata’s wisdom that is beyond seeing, they achieve supreme perfect enlightenment and establish themselves in supernormal powers.
The Buddha said to the Dragon King:
"If a person does not commit sexual misconduct, they will attain the four virtues praised by those of clear wisdom.
What are these four?"
He guards his sense faculties and is free from all frivolous play, so that he is praised by the entire world.
Having abandoned sexual misconduct, no one dares to cast a light or lewd glance upon his wife.
By means of these roots of virtue, one aspires to the unsurpassed, true, and correct path, and attains the mark of a great man: the concealment of the male organ within a sheath.
The Buddha said to the Dragon King:
"When a person does not speak falsely, the devas and the people of the world praise them with eight qualities."
What are the eight?
One’s face shall be pure;
one’s speech shall be such that all people in the world regard it with trust and confidence.
They have personally realized their own realization and are revered by devas and humans;
they harbor supreme sincerity and are free from perverse thoughts;
their minds are pure and free from flattery or deceit.
They experience great joy and are free from weariness or aversion;
they are able to receive prohibitions and instructions without uttering coarse words;
and whether born in the heavens or among humans, they alone are seen as worthy of trust and confidence, being free from doubt.
"Truthful speech is the foundation of virtuous conduct; by aspiring to the unsurpassed, truly correct Way, one will thereby always attain sincerity.
The Buddha said to the Dragon King:
"If a person refrains from double-tongued speech, they will obtain five kinds of non-separation."
What are the five?
One's body is not separated [from its faculties], and there is no distraction;
one's retinue is not dispersed, and one does not treat others with arrogance.
One attains indestructible faith and perceives the retribution of conditions;
one possesses indestructible dharmas in others, taking practice as the essential;
and one attains harmony with friends and kin, because there is no deception.

By means of these roots of virtue, they seek supreme perfect enlightenment; they attain the status of the Tathāgata’s retinue, free from disorder, such that all Māras and adversaries can never destroy the Tathāgata’s retinue.
The Buddha said to the Dragon King:
"If a person refrains from harsh speech, they will receive the retribution of eight kinds of pure speech; after their life ends, they will be reborn in the heavens."

What are the eight? His speech is in accordance with the truth; his speech is gentle; his speech is appropriate; his speech is harmonious; his speech is readily accepted; his speech is radiant; his speech is such that all people receive it with joy; and his speech is not censured by the multitude.
"By virtue of this root of merit, one aspires to the unsurpassed, right, and true Way, and attains the Tathāgata’s voice that transcends Brahmā.
The Buddha said to the Dragon King:
"If a person refrains from frivolous speech, they will attain the three types of right conduct."
What are the three? Constantly bringing clarity to the multitude, being honored and loved by all;
keeping the mind always single-minded, entering into ultimate sincerity; and...
By not indulging in much speech, one shall always attain great honor among devas and humans, never being treated with triviality.

By virtue of these roots of merit, one aspires to the unsurpassed, right, and true path; having received the prediction of Buddhahood, one shall achieve the state of a Tathāgata exactly as spoken, without any discrepancy.
The Buddha said to the Dragon King:
"If a person is free from envy, they will attain five kinds of majestic spiritual power.
What are these five?"
With clarity of body, speech, and mind, and with all faculties complete;
having attained immense wealth, they enjoy themselves at will;
they subdue all enemies and delight in food, drink, and the occupations of fine flavors and living.
His merit and virtue are lofty and sublime; he is honored and revered by all kings, who provide him with protection and shelter.
Possessing exquisite treasures as if they were his own, he brings about extraordinary family merit through the power of past roots of goodness, and he feels no envy for the wealth of others.
Based on these roots of virtue, one aspires to the unsurpassed, true, and correct path, attaining the state of a World-Honored One who is honored by the three realms.
The Buddha said to the Dragon King:
“When a person is free from anger, they attain eight dharmas that gladden the mind.
What are the eight? They are:
delighting in the truth of non-harming, thereby eliminating ill will;
delighting in sincerity, and having no desire for contention in the mind.
The mind delights in sincerity and straightforwardness, being serene and harmonious;
equal toward sages and worthies, it constantly harbors a heart of compassion;

it is endowed with pity and sees others' peace and joy; it is upright and exceptionally beautiful, revered by all people; it finds no difficulty in being reborn in the Brahma Heaven; and because the mind employs skillful means out of a spirit of sorrowful harmony—this is the eighth.

"By means of these eight roots of virtue, one aspires to the unsurpassed, right, and true path of enlightenment, and becomes a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha, who is never weary of contemplation.
The Buddha said to the Dragon King:
"A person who is free from wrong views attains ten dharmic virtues."
What are the ten? They are:
having a sincere and truthful disposition, obtaining virtuous friends;
and believing in the retribution of good and evil.
If their lives have already ended, they do not harm or offend others;
they remain mindful of practicing the Buddha-way with a mind free from distraction;
they do not serve celestial deities, for their will is grounded in sincerity and simplicity.
He abandons the arts of flattery and deceitful incantations;
he forms friendships with devas and humans, but does not take as companions those in the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals;
he stands out preeminent among the multitudes, possessing towering merit, with the Noble Path as his supreme goal.
Free from false views, free from attachment to the body, and free from evil perspectives;
being entirely without hindrance and equal toward the noble ones, they are reborn in the heavens or among humans in an instant.

These are the ten virtuous qualities. Having abandoned false views and attained the foundation, one aspires to the unsurpassed, right, and true path; one draws near to the Dharma of the Buddhas, swiftly attains supernormal powers, and becomes a Tathāgata.
The Buddha said to the Dragon King:

"A bodhisattva who practices giving while remaining free from taking life will constantly attain great wealth, longevity, boundless conduct, and the path of a bodhisattva; no external enemies shall be able to withstand them."

One who has already abandoned theft and practices giving, possessing abundant wealth and treasures that others dare not seize, can practice the bodhisattva path without obstruction or interruption, thereby gathering all dharmas of merit.

One who practices giving while abstaining from sexual misconduct will later always be greatly wealthy; their wife will be free from wanton behavior, no one among humans will dare to offend them, and the women of their household will not look upon others with lustful eyes.

One who practices giving while abstaining from false speech will always possess great wealth and never be subject to slander; they will be protected by even those of inferior status, and as they practice the path of the bodhisattva, their words and deeds will correspond, and their aspirations will be steadfast.

One who practices giving while abstaining from divisive speech will always possess great wealth, and their retinue will not be divided; by practicing the bodhisattva path, they will attain the quality of having a retinue that is entirely upright and even-minded.

One who has already abandoned harsh speech and practices giving will always possess great wealth; their words will be accepted by others, and as they practice the bodhisattva path and enter assemblies, all will rejoice.
One who gives while abstaining from frivolous speech will always possess great wealth; whatever they say will be carried out, and as they practice the bodhisattva path, they will sever all doubts.

One who gives while abstaining from envy will always possess great wealth; they will have an abundance of fine food, clothing, and bedding, and as they practice the bodhisattva path, they will bestow upon others whatever they themselves delight in, thereby attaining great dignity and nobility.

One who practices giving while free from a mind of ill-will will always possess great wealth, be radiant and upright in appearance, have speech that all people cherish, remain free from intent to harm while practicing the bodhisattva path, and be endowed with all the sense faculties.

One who practices giving while free from wrong views will always possess great wealth; established in right view, they will be born into a noble family, encounter Buddhas and World-Honored Ones, practice the bodhisattva path without being separated from the Buddhas, constantly hear the Dharma, and give rise to the bodhicitta.
The Buddha said to the Dragon King:
"This is called the ten wholesome acts of giving; their adornment is so vast!
These ten wholesome practices, adorned by precepts and through the fulfillment of one's own vows, bring about the attainment of all Buddha-dharmas."
Adorned with patience, they perfect the primary marks and secondary characteristics and attain the voice of a Buddha;
adorned with diligence, they subdue demonic adversaries and transcend through the teachings of the Buddha-way;
adorned with meditative concentration, their mental inclinations become pure.
Adorned with wisdom, one eliminates all erroneous views;
adorned with loving-kindness, one should practice benevolence and harmony, refraining from harming sentient beings;
adorned with compassion, one does not abandon the masses.
They practice the adornment of joy, remaining free from weariness or aversion;
they practice the adornment of protection, attaining non-attachment and severing all knots of doubt;
they practice the adornment of benevolence, exhorting and transforming all living beings.
Adorned with the practice of the foundations of mindfulness, one brings rest to all bodily sensations and fulfills the mind and dharmas;
adorned with the practice of the right efforts, one abandons all unwholesome dharmas and fulfills virtuous qualities;
adorned with the bases of supernormal power, one possesses the lightness and agility of the supernormal powers.
Adorned with the five faculties, they make their practice firm; through supreme diligence they remain free from negligence, and by cultivating the mind they eliminate all defilements.
Adorned with the five powers, they subdue and transform all enmities with a straightforward mind.
Adorned with the factors of awakening, they clearly understand all phenomena according to their original source.
Adorned with the eightfold path, they embrace and bring forth right wisdom;
adorned with tranquility, they eliminate all defilements and worldly toil;
adorned with contemplation, they observe the fundamental nature of all phenomena, discerning that they are entirely non-existent.
“Through the adornment of skillful means, whether numbered or unnumbered, conditioned or unconditioned, one is fully endowed with peace and security.
The Buddha said to the Dragon King:
“To speak of the essentials, the virtue of the ten wholesome paths is fully endowed with the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses, thereby accomplishing all the Buddha-dharmas.”
Because they are fully perfected, one should always be diligent in the virtue of these ten wholesome actions, which are universally and magnificently adorned.

Just as the planting, harvesting, and cultivation of the hundred grains, medicinal herbs, trees, flowers, and fruits throughout the provinces, kingdoms, counties, towns, villages, hamlets, and settlements all depend upon the earth;
so too do the virtues of the ten wholesome actions serve as the basis for both the heavens and the human realm.

Whether it be those in training or those beyond training, those who have attained the realization of the fruits, those abiding in the path of the pratyekabuddhas, those practicing the path of the bodhisattvas, or the dharmas of the path of all Buddhas—all arise from following this.
Thereupon, the Dragon King Sāgara addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"What is meant by 'the practice of a bodhisattva who has entered the Dharma-gate'?
To enter the Dharma-gate is to eliminate the offenses of the hindrances of the aggregates from past lives."
"Having already removed the hindrances of the aggregates (skandha-nīvaraṇa), one attains transcendence.
The Buddha said to the Dragon King:
"Bodhisattvas possess one dharma that removes all sinful hindrances."
What is the one? It is to establish oneself in protection, not to abandon what has been taught, and to repent for and confess one's transgressions.
Furthermore, there are two other dharmas that eliminate all veils of sin.
What are these two?
Constantly contemplating pure dharmas and not creating [karmic] conditions in the present.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas that eliminate all veils of sin.
What are these three?
Entering into the wisdom of dependent origination, possessing a joyful mind, and relying on the dharma of primordial purity to realize that all things are fundamentally non-existent.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas that eliminate all hindrances of sin.
What are the four? They are:
thorough understanding of emptiness, not dwelling in the signless, proceeding toward the wishless, and wisdom that performs no conditioned action.
Furthermore, there are five dharmas that eliminate all hindrances of sin.
What are the five? They are:
no self, no person, no life-force, no vital principle, and no consciousness.
Furthermore, there are six dharmas that eliminate all hindrances of sin.
What are the six? They are:
to be joyful and possess firm faith without doubt; to observe with careful discernment in coming and going, advancing and stopping; to act with utmost sincerity; and not to lose right faith.
These are the six dharmas that eliminate all veils of sin.
The Dragon King addressed the Buddha,
saying, "What is meant by a bodhisattva attaining transcendence?
The World-Honored One replied:
“There are ten matters by which a bodhisattva attains transcendence.
What are the ten?
Constant mindfulness and joyful delight;”
The purity of the mind-nature; skillful means;
and firm, vigorous diligence.
Observing sentient beings, one practices boundless compassion;
cultivating virtue without weariness, one pursues extensive learning without fatigue;
and in serving others, one is never negligent.
They shall attend to the site of enlightenment;
they shall cause others to attain the wisdom of a Buddha;
and they shall not abandon the mind of enlightenment.
These are the ten matters by which the conduct of a bodhisattva attains transcendence and distinction.
12. Chapter Twelve: The Prediction of the Asura Yajñaśrestha. Then the asura Yajñaśrestha addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“What is meant by a bodhisattva surpassing all virtues?”
The Buddha told the spirit Aśubha:
"There are eight qualities by which a bodhisattva transcends all other virtues.
What are these eight?"
In this regard, the bodhisattva abandons arrogance and remains humble, submissive, and reverent toward all people;
they receive instruction with deference and compliance, ensuring that their words and deeds correspond, and remain modest and respectful toward their elders and superiors;
taking all virtuous qualities and dharmas as their foundation, their practice is steadfast and surpasses all other wholesome virtues.
They delight in various kinds of sublime giving;
they would rather lose their own bodies and lives than seek out the vulnerabilities of others;
and seeing those in peril or fear, they bestow upon them fearlessness.
Not abandoning those who come for refuge;
never being satisfied with seeking all the karmic activities of merit and wisdom—
these are the eight dharmas.
The Asura General Viśvadeva again asked the Buddha:
"By practicing how many dharmas does a bodhisattva attain a tall and large body, a full and broad face, a flourishing retinue, and an infinitely vast mind?"
The Buddha told the yakṣa Anabhibhūta:
"There are four things by which a bodhisattva attains a large body.
What are these four?"
One does not speak of the greed or envy in the actions of others;
one creates images of the Buddha, complete with all the primary and secondary marks;
and one reconciles those who are divided, encouraging them to resolve their minds upon the unsurpassed, true, and correct path.
To have an appearance that causes no harm toward sentient beings—
these are the four matters by which one attains a large body.
There are four matters by which a bodhisattva’s face becomes broad and full.
What are the four?

Giving various ornaments as alms; giving all that one loves without regret; constantly regarding the Tathāgata with eyes of loving-kindness; and not giving rise to jealousy upon seeing others who are handsome.
These are the four matters by which one attains a full and radiant complexion.
A bodhisattva attains a flourishing retinue through four matters.
What are these four? They are:
to abstain from divisive speech and never to cause the destruction of others' retinues;
Seeing the companions of others, one rejoices on their behalf;
one does not abandon the mind of enlightenment;
and together with others, one transforms them, causing them to resolve upon the path to enlightenment.
These are the four.
There are four matters by which a bodhisattva’s intention becomes infinitely vast. What are these four?
Their minds are pure and free from flattery, having eliminated heavy craving and desire;
they remain untiring amidst all circumstances;
their will is set upon the sublime, as they penetrate deeply into the essential Dharma.
"All dharmas are empty from beginning to end;
these are the four [immeasurables], by which the Bodhisattva’s intention is infinitely vast.

Thereupon, the yakṣa Vihāra-pratiṣṭhita, together with his retinue of thirty-two thousand, each scattered various kinds of eight-thousandfold celestial flowers over the World-Honored One and praised him in verse, saying:
"Should there be immeasurable multitudes of human beings throughout the ten directions who,
in a single moment, were to make offerings to the World-Honored One;
even if all those people in the ten directions were to offer every virtue— "
Even if one were to provide for others with an impartial mind for hundreds of thousands of kalpas,
it could not equal the meritorious practice of compassion and pity;
how then could offerings ever repay that which is as tranquil and ultimate as it ought to be?
This is the offering and service rendered throughout the ten directions;
a resolve to awaken that is peerless, abiding in the true reality as it truly is.
Thus I am autonomous, having established my will free from flattery or deceit.
Having already awakened to the fact that [all things] are fundamentally non-existent, I have personally attained the Way of the Buddha.
The Honored One among Men, seeing my compassion, Is without flattery in the three realms;
May the Ten Powers bear witness to me, Understanding the nature and conduct of my mind.
Supple and free from timidity, having abandoned all fears;
excelling in generosity, self-restraint, and discipline; maintaining precepts and patience;
exerting oneself in meditative concentration; and abiding in accordance with wisdom.
I shall follow with compassion and pity, always upholding the practice of supreme sincerity.

Grant me your pity; it would be better for me not to receive a prediction of goodness than for you, O Honored One among Men, to grant it to me alone. I shall instead receive my own individual prediction from the Buddha.
"I have no doubts at all; I do not consider myself to have attained freedom.
I have clearly realized the ultimate truth, and my pure resolve lies in the Way.
At that time, the Honored One among Men smiled, and Yueying immediately asked:
"Why do you now smile with joy?
Only you, O Holy One, can explain this.
At that time, the one who had manifested and transformed him said:
“Listen attentively, Yueying, to why I have manifested this display and emitted this great radiance.
At that time, when I dwelt in seclusion, my aspiration was for the sublime Great Way;
there were thirty-two thousand people, along with all their retinues, who followed me.”
Throughout hundreds of thousands of kalpas, they shall constantly practice the bodhisattva path;
with all their aspirations equal and identical, they shall attain the holy path of the Buddhas.
They shall make offerings to all Buddhas, as numerous as the sands along the banks of the Ganges.
The number of people he transforms and guides exceeds even this.
That eon is called Joyful, and is also named Pure and Further Pure;
there he attains Buddhahood as Free from Dust and Tranquil, awakening to the ultimate state beyond sorrow.
This one, dwelling in seclusion and being vast and universal, shall become a Dharma King;
through the power of transcendent diligence, he shall be named Imperial Banner.
His world shall be called Joyful, Benevolent, and Adorned.
Abundant and inexpensive food and clothing, like those in the Tuṣita Heaven;
the lifespan of that One of Ten Powers will be seven billion years,
reaching a full sixty nayutas, along with bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs.
The assembly of bodhisattvas numbered eight hundred nayutas;
firmly established in dhāraṇī, they fully understood everything they heard.
During that Joyful Eon, he was also known as Pure and Further Pure.
Through such analogies as these, they shall all attain the honored path of the Buddha.
They transform and enlighten hundreds of thousands of people, causing them all to abide in the Buddha-way.
Fully observing this supreme excellence is the bodhisattva’s mind of the Way.
While dwelling in seclusion without a tutelary deity, they heard the Buddha bestow his prediction;
the great assembly of forty million beings all resolved their minds upon Bodhisattvahood.
The three-thousandfold world system shook, and at that moment, celestial flowers rained down from the sky.
Excellent is this essential virtue, That which is maintained by the mind.
Chapter Thirteen: The Prophecy of the Dragon King Avīta (The Unburnt). At that time, the Dragon King Avīta addressed the Buddha, saying:
“All dharmas are entirely without abiding, and there is no person.”
"How can there be one who receives the prediction [of enlightenment]?
Who shall attain the unsurpassed, perfect, true path and become a Most Perfectly Awakened One?
The Buddha said:
"It is so! It is as you have said:
'All dharmas abide nowhere, and there is no person.'"
"All dharmas are likewise thus. Foolish ordinary people dwell in perversion;
abiding in the notions of self and person, they conceive the notion of a person where no person exists."
The Bodhisattvas give rise to great compassion in order to eliminate inversions and remove the notions of self, person, and individual; they don the armor of awakened virtue.
These true beings understand that all phenomena are devoid of self or person, yet they instruct, transform, and establish sentient beings through the concepts of self and person.
Regarding what you, O virtuous ones, have asked:
"Who is it that receives the prediction?"—
if you, all virtuous ones, understand that persons are empty and devoid of self, then you shall receive the prediction.
To contemplate all dharmas as equal and all dharmas as quiescent is to receive the prediction of enlightenment;
to regard all Buddha-lands as equal and to have nothing to grasp, with a mind pure and free from defilement, is to receive the prediction of enlightenment;
to observe all Buddhas with wisdom as equal and the path of the Buddhas as not destroying the dharma-realm is to receive the prediction of enlightenment.

Regarding all the hosts of Māras and every form of Māra, when one has realized that the mind is fundamentally free from both dust and non-dust, one receives the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).

To be without name and without mark, without response and without non-response, without thought and without non-thought, and without accepting or rejecting—this is receiving the prediction of enlightenment.
The Buddha said to the Dragon King:
"When the mind, intellect, and consciousness have no place of abiding or establishment, that is the reception of the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).

All phenomena are thus; because all phenomena are fundamentally true through the absence of causes and conditions, one awakens to the equality and non-differentiation of all phenomena, thereby accomplishing the unsurpassed, perfect, and true path."

Seeking the ultimate source, there is neither the receiving of a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) nor the attainment of the Buddha-way, whether it be one who receives a prediction or one who has already received it. Why is this?
All dharmas are formless; their beginning and end are entirely severed, and they all lack a master.
All dharmas evolve from causes and conditions; all dharmas are like space, because they lack the characteristic of arising;
all dharmas lack the characteristic of arising, because they lack the characteristic of going;
all dharmas have no place from which they come, because their fundamental nature is empty.
All dharmas have no destination, because they have not yet been originated;
all dharmas have no abode, because no location can be apprehended;
all dharmas are entirely empty, because they lack substantiality.
All dharmas are without attachment, because they have no dependence;
all dharmas have nothing upon which to depend, because they are immovable;
all dharmas are immovable, because they have no location.
All dharmas are deluded, because they are spontaneous;
all dharmas are spontaneous, because they are beyond verbal instruction;
all dharmas are beyond verbal instruction, because they are devoid of form or image.
All phenomena are formless, because they are free from thought;
all phenomena are without thought, because they are without causes and conditions;
all phenomena are without causes and conditions, because they have no sphere of activity.
All dharmas have no activity, because they are quiescent;
all dharmas are quiescent, because there are no aggregates of sensation;
all dharmas have no aggregates of sensation, because they are fundamentally pure and empty.
All dharmas have the characteristic of liberation, because they are non-dual;
all dharmas are non-dual, because they are fundamentally one;
all dharmas are fundamentally one, because they are free from multiplicity.
"All dharmas are equal and without distinction, because they are awakened through equality.
The Buddha said to the Dragon King:
"To understand that all dharmas are equal means there is no one who receives the prediction of enlightenment, nor is there anyone who achieves equal awakening."

Furthermore, observe this: the Tathāgata is steadfast, giving rise to infinite compassion, as well as the power of encouragement and joy from all the bodhisattvas. Such are all dharmas; he explains them for the sake of countless beings, yet those who assemble are finite in number.
In the contemplation of all dharmas, there is no person who attains liberation, nor are dharmas transcended.

The person is suchness; the Dharma is suchness; the Path is suchness; the Buddha is suchness; the decision [of Nirvana] is suchness; and all dharmas are suchness. Therefore, he is called the Tathāgata.

Having realized that all is fundamentally non-existent (*mūla-abhāva*), and because one abides in this fundamental non-existence, one cannot be moved; therefore, it is called "fundamental non-existence.
Since there is no image of fundamental non-existence and no destruction of fundamental non-existence, and because one has fully understood this fundamental non-existence, one is called a Tathāgata.
Because of the Tathāgata, one abides equally in original non-being; all dharmas are likewise equal to this abiding in original non-being—this is the ground of the Tathāgata’s equal abiding.
Any bodhisattva who hears this teaching and is neither terrified nor frightened, neither afraid nor daunted, shall explain it for others as the ground of the Tathāgata’s equal abiding.

When the Buddha had spoken these words, three thousand bodhisattvas all attained the patience of the Dharma (dharmanidhyāna-kṣānti). The Dragon King Anavatapta leaped for joy and, with a white pearl necklace whose value equaled that of this entire world, covered the Buddha.

Chapter 14: The Woman Jewel Jin Receiving the Prediction of Enlightenment (Part Three) At that time, the Dragon King Sāgara had a daughter named Ratnapaṭṭadharā-vimalapaṭṭā. She was upright and beautiful, her countenance radiant and exquisite. Accompanied by ten thousand dragon ladies, each holding a pearl necklace in her right hand, she gazed at the Buddha with single-minded devotion, her eyes never blinking, as she prostrated before him and stood.
Then the woman Baojin and the ten thousand ladies presented pearl necklaces to the World-Honored One and, with one voice, praised him, saying:
"Today we, as a single group, have attained an even mind and have all resolved to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path!"
"In future ages, may we become Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas; may we preach the Dharma and protect the Saṅgha, just as the present Tathāgata does!"
Then the Venerable Mahākāśyapa said to the woman and the ladies-in-waiting:
"Unsurpassed perfect enlightenment is extremely difficult to attain; one cannot achieve the path of Buddhahood in a female body."
The maiden Ratnapaṭṭā said to Mahākāśyapa:
"The mind and will are fundamentally pure; for one who practices as a bodhisattva, attaining Buddhahood is not difficult!
Once they have resolved upon the path to enlightenment, achieving Buddhahood is like looking at the palm of one's hand."
"By being thus able to give rise to the mind of all-encompassing wisdom and insight, one immediately encompasses all Buddha-dharmas.
The woman said to Kāśyapa:
"Furthermore, as it has been said:"
"One cannot attain the path to Buddhahood in a female body;
nor can it be attained in a male body! Why is this so?"
As for that mind of the Way, it is neither male nor female.
As the Buddha has said:
"In reckoning the eye, there is neither male nor female."
The same applies to the ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind; they likewise have neither male nor female.
Why is this? It is because, O virtuous one, the eye is empty.
Regarding the reckoning of emptiness: there is neither male nor female; the ears, nose, mouth, body, and mind are all empty. Thus, this voidness and stillness are without male or female.
If one can understand and discern the fundamental nature of the eye, it is called the Way.
It is the same for the ear, nose, mouth, body, and mind. As for reckoning the Way, there is neither the dharma of male nor the dharma of female.
"Therefore, Kāśyapa, just as all dharmas are of the nature of spontaneity (*svabhāva*), the Way is also spontaneous, and I too am spontaneous.
Kāśyapa asked the woman:
"Are you the Way? The woman replied,
"Venerable elder, do you mean to say that I am not the Way?"
Kāśyapa replied, "I am not a follower of the Buddha-way; I am merely a śrāvaka.
The woman asked again:
"Who has brought you to enlightenment? He replied, "The Tathāgata."
The woman asked,
"Even if the Tathāgata were not to attain perfect enlightenment, would he still be able to transform and guide those of venerable age? He replied:
"No. "Therefore, virtuous one, you should know that for those who are there, it is by means of the Way, and there is nothing that does not awaken to the Way.
Kāśyapa asked the girl:
"Is contrariness the Way?
He replied, "Indeed it is, Kāśyapa!"
To go against [the flow] is the Way. Why is this so?

Because one can awaken to and understand original purity through such opposition; as for the Way, there is no understanding that involves opposition, yet to oppose original purity is what is called the Way.
Emptiness is fundamentally without discrimination; thus, all adversities are called the Way.
If phenomena were subject to conjunction or dispersion, they would not be the Way.
Only that which treats all phenomena with equanimity and accords with reality as it is constitutes the Way.
Kāśyapa asked the girl,
"Who bestowed such eloquence upon you?
The girl replied:
“Venerable Kāśyapa has bestowed eloquence upon me.
Even if you, O worthy one, had not questioned me, for what reason would this eloquence have arisen?
For example, Kāśyapa!”
"If there is no one to call out, by what cause would there be an echo?
Likewise, if there were no one to inquire about the meaning of the Bodhisattva, there would be no basis for the arising of eloquence.
Kāśyapa asked the girl:
“How many Buddhas have you made offerings to?
The woman replied,
“As many as the afflictions you, O Noble One, have severed.”
Kāśyapa replied to the woman,
“I do not sever the afflictions.
The woman asked again:
“Virtuous one!
Is there defilement and impurity in the secular world? Kāśyapa replied:
"I have no afflictions, nor do I sever them.
The woman asked again,
"Where do you place all the afflictions?"
He replied: “Neither arising nor ceasing, and there is nothing to be established.
Such is my understanding; it is as it was originally, non-existent.”
He asked again:
"Can 'original non-existence' (mūla-abhāva) truly be known? He replied:
"No, [it is not so]. He asked again:
"For what reason do you say this, O Virtuous One?"
"His wisdom is like the Path; it is as he understands what is known.
"He clarifies the unconditioned and knows it thus; because he understands that it is fundamentally non-existent, his wisdom is therefore said to be equal to that of ordinary people."
He asked the woman again:
"Does that which you have articulated cut off all speech? She replied:
"I have nothing to sever, nor is there anything to be spoken.
Why is this? The Dharma-realm has nothing to be severed; all that is taught accords with the Dharma-realm."
Kāśyapa asked the woman again:
"Do you not have doubts regarding my being equal to ordinary persons?
The woman replied:
“If the dharmas of the wisdom of ordinary persons established by you were each different, I would have doubts.
However, I maintain that the dharmas of ordinary persons are not different; therefore, I have no doubts.”
"All dharmas are equal because they are not manifold; this is called equality. Just as space is, so is it called equality.
He then asked the woman:
"Are you equal toward ordinary people and toward sages?"
He replied: "I am neither an ordinary man, nor am I a sage or a worthy one. Why is this so?
"If we were equal to ordinary worldlings, we would not practice as Bodhisattvas;
if we were equal to the noble ones, we would sever the Buddha-dharma.
He then asked the woman:
"If you are neither equal to ordinary worldlings nor equal to noble sages,
are you then equal to the Buddha? The woman replied, "No!"
"Why is this? Because my own body is fundamentally equal to the Buddha-dharma.
He then asked the woman:
"If you were equal to the Buddha’s Dharma, would you not have attained the Buddha’s Dharma?
The woman replied, "Venerable sir,
do you believe that the Buddha’s Dharma has coming, going, or exists in the present through conditions?"
"Does it have spatial dimensions?
Does it occupy a location as blue, yellow, red, white, or black?
He replied to the woman:
"The Dharma of all Buddhas has no form or appearance.
The woman replied,
"If the Dharma of all Buddhas has no form or appearance, why do you seek it from me?"
Kāśyapa asked the girl,
“Where should one seek the Buddha-dharma? She replied:
"One should seek it within the sixty-two views.
He asked again:
"Within what should the sixty-two views be sought?"
He replied: "One should seek it within the liberation of the Tathāgata.
He asked again:
"Where should one seek the liberation of the Tathāgata? He replied,
"One should seek it within the five heinous crimes."
He asked again:
"Where should one seek the five heinous crimes? He replied:
"One should seek it within the knowledge and vision of deliverance.
He asked again: "What does this mean?"
The woman replied:
"Neither bound nor liberated, neither grasped nor relinquished—this is primordial purity. This is the profound teaching regarding all phenomena; it is not a matter of mere words."
He asked the woman again,
"Does this teaching of yours not contradict the words of the Tathāgata?
The woman replied:
"This is the word of ultimate truth; it does not contravene or lose the teaching of the Tathāgata. Why is this so?
Because the path of the Tathāgata is such that there is nothing to be attained, nothing to be maintained, and no verbal expression."
All that is spoken is but sound; yet one who understands the root of the Way knows that there is no sound therein.
O Benevolent One!
Understand that the Way is quiescent and traceless, yet you take names and traces as your own cherished traces.
Kāśyapa asked again:
"If the Way is traceless, how can such characteristics as these constitute the attainment of supreme perfect enlightenment? He replied:
"Furthermore, one does not attain supreme perfect enlightenment through the body, nor does one attain it through the mind. Why is this?
It is because the Way is realized only when both body and mind are spontaneously natural."
"That which is natural has no perception at all; I take this to be the Way, yet I do not consider it to be the Way by which one achieves supreme perfect enlightenment.
Kāśyapa asked the girl:
"If you have established this as the Way, why do you not turn the Wheel of Dharma?"
The woman replied,
"I am merely turning the Wheel of Dharma! Kāśyapa asked:
"What kind of wheel of Dharma is being turned?
The woman replied,
"It is the immovable wheel, which is far removed from all forms of attachment and dwelling."
That which is called the wheel of Dharma is so named because it abides in the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
That which is the wheel of primordial non-existence is so named because it accords with primordial non-existence.
That which is the wheel of non-interruption is so named because it abides in original purity, just as it was.
The wheel of non-attachment is so called because it realizes all phenomena without any clinging.
The wheel of non-duality is so called because it is equal toward all phenomena.
The wheel of non-multiplicity is so called because it endures the single practice.
The Wheel of the Wordless transforms all sounds such that they are entirely free from conceptualization, for they enter into the single flavor.
The Pure Wheel is so called because it is entirely free from defilement.
The wheel that severs all that is undisciplined exists because neither permanence nor impermanence can be apprehended.
The wheel that is without confusion exists because of the skillful observation of karmic retribution.
The wheel of utmost sincerity exists because there is neither arising nor ceasing.
The wheel of emptiness and non-existence is so called because it is signless and wishless. O Kāśyapa!
Since the wheel is thus, what is there to be turned?
Mahākāśyapa said, "With such eloquence as yours,
you shall before long attain unsurpassed, perfect, true, and complete enlightenment!
The woman replied:
"Even if Kāśyapa should attain supreme perfect enlightenment, I too shall attain supreme perfect enlightenment! Kāśyapa replied:
"I shall never attain supreme perfect enlightenment!"
The woman replied, “One who thus realizes the Dharma-body dwells in the Way without dwelling anywhere; there is nothing that can be attained, yet one achieves supreme perfect enlightenment.
When the woman spoke these words, five hundred bodhisattvas attained the patience of the Dharma (dharmakṣānti).
The Buddha then praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! You have eloquently expounded this Dharma!"
At that time, the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and kinnaras within the assembly thought to themselves:
"When will this maiden Ratnapaṭṭikā attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
The Buddha, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the devas, nāgas, spirits, and gandharvas, addressed the bhikṣus:

"Three hundred incalculable kalpas from now, this maiden Ratnapaṭṭa shall attain Buddhahood; her name shall be Samantaprabhā Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. Her world shall be called Prabhā, and the kalpa shall be called Viśuddha."
"In that world of Radiance, the light of the Tathāgata shall be perpetually and greatly brilliant.
There will be ninety-two billion bodhisattvas, and the Buddha’s lifespan shall be ten intermediate kalpas.
Thereupon, the Ten Thousand Dragon Queens addressed the Buddha, saying:
"When the Tathāgata Viśvabhū attains Buddhahood, we vow to be born in that land!
The Buddha then prophesied that they would indeed be born in that land.
Chapter Fifteen: Śakra Devendra (3). Thereupon, Śakra Devendra addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"These gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven constantly harbor fear; they lack benevolent deities.
When the gods battle with the asuras, they contend with one another, harboring grudges and each possessing the poison of hatred."

"I only pray that the World-Honored One, out of compassion for sentient beings, will cause all the unwholesome deities to assemble here, and that all these gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven will be made to harmonize together!
The Buddha addressed the unwholesome deity Yanju Wushan and the unwholesome deity Kuangzha Chaodu Liugujin, saying: "O worthy ones!
This mind of benevolence is praised by all Buddhas.
If a person can practice compassion, they will be fully endowed with benefit and meaning in both the present life and future lives.
This life is exceedingly short; one must eventually pass on to the next world.
Where there is meeting, there must be separation; kingdoms, lands, and noble status all return to impermanence.

Your bodies, too, cannot escape this affliction; you should contemplate the afterlife, remain harmonious and of one mind, harbor no anger, and guard against the karmic conditions of both sin and merit.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke words of bitter sorrow and compassion, causing the asuras and the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to reach a complete reconciliation.
Each of them declared:
"From this day forward, we shall act as friends and accord with impartial conduct; each of us shall harbor a heart of pity and compassion, free from any thought of malice."
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, excellent, O worthy ones!
"This is the foremost way to make offerings to the Tathāgata, for it is practiced through the cultivation of loving-kindness.
When these words were spoken, that which was taught as the merit of collective harmony and non-contention is called the Samādhi of Loving-Kindness.
“There are four matters for honoring and respecting the Tathāgata.
What are the four?
Not transgressing the precepts;”
To practice kindness through body, speech, and mind;
not to sever the continuity of the Three Jewels, but to be intent upon the Buddha-way;
and to expound for others the Dharma as it has been heard.
"These are the four matters by which one honors and reveres the Tathāgata as an act of offering.
Thereupon, twenty-three thousand devas and *asura* spirits within the assembly, having heard these words, all resolved to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path.

The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Dragon King of the Sea, Scroll Four.

Chapter 16: The Chapter on the Golden-Winged Birds (4) The Sixteenth Chapter:

The Chapter on the Golden-Winged Birds At that time, there were four dragon kings—first named Āśvāsa (Inhaling), second named Mahāśvāsa (Great Inhaling), third named Ṛkṣa (Bear), and fourth named Anantavarṇa (Infinite Color)—who addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

"Within this great ocean, there are countless species of dragons who have come to be born here as a result of various karmic actions and causal conditions. Some belong to the great species, while others belong to the small species; some are weak and inferior, and thus they alone are subjected to contempt and insult."
There are four kinds of garuḍas who constantly devour these nāgas, as well as their wives and children, causing terror among all species of nāgas in the ocean.
We pray that the Buddha will protect them, so that all the nāgas of the sea may always attain peace and security, and harbor no fear.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One removed his black robe and addressed the Dragon King Sāgara:
"You should take this black robe of the Tathāgata and distribute it among all the dragon kings so that it reaches them all."
Why is this so? Because within the great ocean, even one who possesses but a single thread cannot be harmed or disturbed by the King of the Golden-Winged Birds (Garuda). Why is this so?
"Those who uphold the prohibitive precepts will surely obtain their wishes.
At that time, all the great dragon kings were filled with alarm and fear, each thinking to themselves:
"This Buddha’s black robe is extremely small; how could it possibly cover all the dragons throughout the great ocean?"
At that time, the Buddha, knowing the doubts and fears in the minds of the dragon kings, addressed the Dragon King Sāgara:
"Even if all the people throughout the trichiliocosm were each to divide the Tathāgata’s black robe among themselves, it would never be diminished or exhausted."
If one wishes to take up robes, they are like space; according to whatever is desired, they arise spontaneously.
The inconceivable and sublime virtues established by the Buddha are just like this!

Then the Dragon King Sāgara immediately took the Buddha’s robe and divided it himself into countless hundreds of thousands of pieces. He distributed these portions one by one to the dragon kings; according to the dimensions—whether broad or narrow, large or small—of each dragon king’s palace, the robe was naturally provided to them. Yet the robe remained as it was, never known to be exhausted.
At that time, the Dragon King Sāgara addressed the various dragon kings:
"You should revere this robe as you would revere the World-Honored One, and as you would revere a stupa or a monastery. Why is this so?..."
This robe is that which the Tathāgata wore; for this reason, it should be revered just as one honors a stūpa or a monastery.
Even if one were to make every possible offering to the Tathāgata, there would be no distinction between such offerings and the honoring of this robe.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One addressed the Dragon King Sāgara:
"So it is, so it is! It is just as you have said!"
"One who receives this robe makes an offering to the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, observe how the various dragons, as well as their wives and children, each divide the Tathāgata’s robe.
They replied:
“Yes, indeed, I have seen it!
The Buddha said:

“I have bestowed upon them all the prediction of enlightenment, so that they shall immediately be released from their dragon bodies. Within this Bhadrakalpa, with the exception of those who are resolved toward the Mahāyāna, all the other dragons shall attain non-attachment and enter parinirvāṇa.”
Thus it is, O Dragon King!

While the Tathāgata remains in the world, if any among the multitudes of beings gives rise to a single thought of goodness, they will, by that condition, attain Buddhahood; there has never been a failure in this regard.
At that time, the various nāgas in the ocean, along with their wives and offspring, were filled with joy and delight; they threw themselves before the Buddha and spoke with one voice, saying:
"That which the Tathāgata speaks is ultimately without duality; it is sincere and not false. Grant us this prediction of future enlightenment, leading us to the attainment of the unconditioned."

Today we dwell within the great ocean; we take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the assembly of noble ones, receive and uphold the prohibitive precepts, and reverently comply with the Tathāgata’s repeated teachings.
While the Tathāgata is present in the world, they go to him repeatedly; having seen the Buddha, they prostrate themselves and listen to and gather his teachings.
After his parinirvāṇa, they make offerings to his relics, serving the relics of the World-Honored One with every kind of requisite.

Thereupon, the four kings of the garuḍas, having heard what the Buddha had established, were struck with alarm and hurried to the place where the Buddha was. Prostrating themselves at his feet, they said:
"For what reason, World-Honored One, have you taken away our food?"
The Buddha said:
"There are four kinds of nutriment that lead to rebirth in three destinations.
What are the four?"

The first is to hunt birds and beasts with nets, to cruelly harm the multitude of livestock, and to kill living beings and deprive them of life for the sake of food and drink; this leads to rebirth in evil realms.

The second is to carry weapons such as swords, spears, axes, and lances to strike, stab, coerce, and shoot, and to plunder the wealth of others for the sake of food and drink; this leads to rebirth in evil realms.
The third is to obtain food through stinginess, greed, flattery, and deceit; through agitation, violation of prohibitions, false views, and clever trickery—this leads to an evil destination.

The fourth is to obtain food by falsely claiming to be a teacher when one is not, falsely claiming to be a World-Honored One when one is not, falsely claiming to be on the right path when one has fallen into error, falsely claiming to be a śramaṇa when one is not, falsely claiming to be pure when one is not, and falsely claiming to be a practitioner of the holy life (brahmacarya) when one is not—thus seeking food through self-deception.
These are the four kinds of nutriment that lead one to dwell in and approach the three evil realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.
The Dharma I teach is for the purpose of eliminating these four nutriments; one should not use them to nourish the body or harm the lives of other sentient beings.

Why is this? Because all sentient beings cherish their own lives and none hate themselves; for this reason, those who wish to protect their own bodies should protect others and bring peace and security to all sentient beings.
"The wise are thus: they do not coerce others with peril; that which ought not to be done, one must be careful never to do!
At that time, the four Garuḍa kings, each accompanied by a thousand followers, addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Today we take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. We confess and repent for the transgressions and calamities committed in the past. We shall uphold the prohibitions and precepts, and from this day forward, we will constantly bestow the gift of fearlessness upon all nāgas. We shall protect the True Dharma until the Buddha-Dharma endures, following the Path of the Dharma until its final extinction, never deviating from the Buddha's teachings."
The Buddha addressed the four Garuḍa kings:
"In the time of the Buddha Suvarṇabhadra, your bodies were those of four bhikṣus named Prīti, Mahāprīti, Uttara, and Uttaramitra."

These four bhikṣus violated the precepts and the Dharma; they were greedy for offerings, their wills were deluded and intoxicated, and they followed after their kinsmen and sought out the powerful and noble. Their minds were distracted by the notion of self, they fell into false views, and they treated other bhikṣus with contempt, harassing and distressing them. They failed to guard their body, speech, and mind, committing many evils. Yet, because they had made incalculable offerings to the Buddha Suvarṇabhadra, for this reason they did not fall into hell, but instead fell among these birds and beasts.
"In the past and present, the killings they have committed are beyond measure; filled with much terror, they have no means of self-protection.

At that moment, the World-Honored One immediately manifested his supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) in accordance with their forms, causing the four garuḍas to remember their past lives and the offerings they had made to the Buddha Kanakamuni and his disciples.
At that time, he recollected all the merits and demerits he had committed; with his own eyes, he beheld everything he had done in previous lives. He addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"My mind was stubborn and difficult to subdue; because it was mired in greed and envy, I caused much harm and violated the teachings of the Honored One, the Golden Benevolent One."
"From this day forward, we would rather lose our lives than dare to commit evil!
The Buddha preached the sutra for them and granted them this prediction:
"At the time of Maitreya Buddha, you shall all attain liberation in his first assembly!"
Chapter 17: On the Relics (4). Chapter Seventeen on the Relics. At that time, the Prince of the Sea Dragon and all the dragons addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is unprecedented!
World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata has spoken for the universal peace of all; he has bestowed the prediction of enlightenment upon the dragons and transformed their retinues so that they all resolve to attain the Way.
Furthermore, by extending his grace, he requested the gift of these black robes to be distributed among the dragons.
Each made offerings and prostrated themselves in service.

By this cause, they attained protection and gave rise to the aspiration for enlightenment; they took pity on sentient beings and observed the four immeasurable minds—loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; they promoted the four debts of gratitude, practiced benevolent giving and loving-kindness, and sought to benefit others equally with all, gathering them together in universal salvation.

By virtue of these practices, sand does not fall upon his body and he remains free from all afflictions; furthermore, when his mind is tranquil, he does not lose his celestial form, and even when transformed into a venomous snake, he is not encountered by a frog while seeking food, nor is he seized and eaten by the King of the Golden-Winged Birds.

The Buddha transformed the four birds so that they all recognized their past lives. During the time of the Buddha Kāśyapa, they were four bhikṣus who, while sitting in meditation, committed acts of violence and did not follow the True Dharma, thereby persecuting their fellow practitioners. Consequently, they fell as garuḍas. From the start, they repented their transgressions, changed their minds and altered their conduct, and resolved to attain the Great Way. Practicing the four immeasurable minds, they did no harm to living beings; having attained this wholesome protection, we are forever at peace and shall no longer be preyed upon. Our wills are free from fear, and throughout the long night there are no hardships—all of us receive the Buddha’s grace.
Now the Tathāgata has accepted the invitation of the Dragon King, and the teaching he has expounded is vast and all-encompassing, like space which covers everything without exception.

Now that the World-Honored One returns to Jambudvīpa, the dragons in the ocean have no one to rely upon or look up to; may you therefore extend great compassion. At the time of your parinirvāṇa, please leave your entire bodily relics in this great ocean so that all classes of beings may offer them flowers, incense, music, garments, banners, and streamers, thereby increasing their merit and swiftly shedding their dragon bodies to quickly attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path.
"I have continued to receive deliverance; it is solely due to the Buddha’s compassionate grace, and with his majestic virtue added thereto, my wishes shall bear fruit.
The Buddha said, "Excellent! It shall be according to your aspiration!"
At that time, Subhūti said to the sons of the nāgas:
"O worthy ones, do not conceive such a thought, for it will obstruct and cause the abandonment of all merit. Why is this so?

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, his relics will be distributed throughout the eight directions. Devas and nāgas above and below, spirits and ghosts, all people, crawling creatures, breathing beings, and all classes of sentient beings—humans and non-humans alike—shall all offer incense, flowers, and music, prostrate themselves, and take refuge. Through transformations and the manifestation of light, those who behold them shall rejoice, knowing that the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power is sublime and infinite.
Relying on this faith, they all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path;
some became pratyekabuddhas, some attained the stage of śrāvaka, some were reborn in the heavens, and others returned to human form to encounter the Dharma, attaining liberation life after life;
by such reckoning, they all universally received salvation.

Now, each of you ministers has made his own aspiration, wishing for the Buddha, the World-Honored One, to enter parinirvāṇa within the great ocean so that he alone may receive the full relics and attend to them.
"For what reason would all sentient beings attain liberation?
They would be forever beset by poverty and distress, with not a single one to provide protection!

For this reason, I say: do not give rise to such a thought as to cause the Buddha, the World-Honored One, to enter parinirvāṇa within the ocean, so that you alone may receive and enshrine his entire śarīra for offerings!"
The nāgas replied: “O Subhūti, do not speak such words!
Do not limit the infinite wisdom of the Tathāgata with the restricted knowledge of your own person.”

The Tathāgata’s meritorious and noble path is sovereign; there is nothing it does not manifest, no distance is too great or too near, and no distinction between "that" and "this. It wanders everywhere throughout the ten directions, as vast as empty space.

In the mere instant of forming this thought, he is able to cause all the palaces of the nāga deities within the ocean, as well as the provinces, prefectures, kingdoms, counties, towns, villages, hamlets, human wildernesses, celestial realms, and worlds of the triple-thousand great thousandfold world system, to each manifest the complete relics of a Buddha and offer every form of worship; yet there is neither increase nor decrease in the body of the Buddha.
He divides his body throughout the countless buddha-lands of the ten directions, yet there is no division; he manifests everywhere, neither departing nor arriving.
For example, just as the reflection of the sun appears in water, the Buddha neither arises nor passes into parinirvāṇa; how then can one seek to limit the wisdom of the Tathāgata?
To seek to limit the Tathāgata is to seek to limit empty space.
At that time, Subhūti, having heard the sons of the nāgas extol the virtues of the Tathāgata as being inexhaustible, boundless, and beyond all analogy, remained silent and spoke no word.
The nāgas of the ocean, the devas in the void, and the various ghosts and spirits leaped for joy and, with great delight, all resolved to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment.
At that time, the Buddha praised the dragon sons, saying:

reaching the finality, there is no boundary of accomplishment.

Chapter 20: Entrustment and Upholding (4). Chapter Twenty: Entrustment and Upholding. Thereupon, the World-Honored One addressed the great beings, saying: "O noble sons!

Immediately, twenty thousand bodhisattvas and ten thousand devaputras rose and stood before the Buddha, speaking with one voice to the World-Honored One:
"We shall receive such a sūtra as this and cause it to be circulated, spreading it far and wide throughout all regions."
The Buddha asked again:
"How do you govern the Dharma and uphold this unsurpassed, true, and correct path of the Tathāgata?
There was a bodhisattva there named Prajñāketudhvaja who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Yes, indeed, World-Honored One!
Since all dharmas, when closely examined, are entirely without anything to be grasped, how could one possibly even remotely grasp the Buddha-way?
The World-Honored One replied:
“Son of good family!

I do not perceive the dharmas of ordinary beings, nor do I perceive the dharmas of those in training or those beyond training; I do not perceive the dharmas of pratyekabuddhas or bodhisattvas, nor do I perceive the dharmas of the Buddhas. Do I possess the dharmas of the Tathāgata?

The Bodhisattva Sarvadharmāpraṇihita said: "O World-Honored One!

The Bodhisattva Animiṣa said:

The World-Honored One said:

The Bodhisattva Anupalambha said:

He replied: "O son of noble family!
This should be tranquil."
The Bodhisattva Nowhere Abiding said:
"Yes, World-Honored One!

He replied: "Son of good family!
This should be tranquil."
The Bodhisattva Gaganagañja said:
“Yes, World-Honored One!
When one contemplates all phenomena as being equal to space, not perceiving those phenomena as anything to be grasped or maintained—does this constitute the protection of all phenomena?”
He replied: "Son of good family!
This should be tranquil."
The Bodhisattva Du Jingang said:
"O World-Honored One!
Is it by not destroying the dharma-realm, yet entering both the realm of persons and the dharma-realm, that one upholds the true Dharma?"
He replied: "Noble son! This should be tranquil."
The Bodhisattva Acyutapada said: "O World-Honored One!
Is one who is unmoved by any phenomena, and who does not rely upon either dharma or non-dharma, one who upholds the true Dharma?"
He replied: "Son of good family!
This should be tranquil."
The Bodhisattva Chao Mo said: “World-Honored One,

when one reaches the realm of Māra and the realm of the Buddha, does one enter the sphere of all dharmas within both the realm of the Buddha and the realm of Māra in order to protect the True Dharma?”
He replied: "Son of good family!
This should be tranquil."
The Bodhisattva Asaṅga said:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!
Since there is absolutely nothing to be attained among all phenomena, and the sound of the Dharma issues from every pore, is this for the sake of protecting the True Dharma?”
He replied: "Son of good family!
This should be tranquil."
The Bodhisattva Samantaśānta said:
"O World-Honored One!

He replied: "Son of good family!
This should be tranquil."
The Bodhisattva Sāgaramati said:
“Yes, World-Honored One!
Is it by means of the ocean-seal that equalizes all dharmas, practicing the taste of all liberations and knowing them to be spontaneous, that one protects the Dharma?”
He replied: "Son of good family! This is naturally so."
The devaputra Susīma said:
“Yes, World-Honored One!

He replied: "Son of good family!
This should be tranquil."
The Devaputra Vimalaprabha said:
"Yes, World-Honored One!

He replied, “Noble son! This should be tranquil.”
The Devaputra Duren said: "Yes, World-Honored One!

When one delivers sentient beings, being unaware of their categories and types, there is no deliverance in what is delivered. Since there is already that which is delivered, it manifests as circulating and returning without abiding in either this or that; does this constitute receiving the Dharma?"
He replied, “Noble son! This should be tranquil.”
The Devaputra Worthy King said:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!

He replied: "Son of good family!

The Devaputra Īśvara said:
"O World-Honored One!

He replied: "Son of good family!
This should be tranquil."
The Devaputra Sunetra said:
“Yes, World-Honored One!

He replied: "Son of good family!
This should be tranquil."

He replied: "Noble daughter! This should be tranquil."

He replied: “Noble daughter! This should be tranquil.”

He replied: "Noble daughter! This should be in silence."
